questions.stem: The void ratio of a soil is defined as the ratio of:
options: Volume of voids to volume of solids
Volume of voids to total volume
Volume of water to volume of voids
Volume of air to volume of voids
questions.solution:
**Volume of voids to volume of SOLIDS.**

> **e = V_v / V_s**

The distinction from **porosity** is the whole point of the question:

| Quantity | Definition | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Void ratio e** | V_v / **V_s** — referred to the volume of **SOLIDS** | **CAN exceed 1** |
| **Porosity n** | V_v / **V** — referred to the **TOTAL** volume | **CANNOT exceed 1** |

Because the denominator of e is only the solid fraction, a very loose soil can have more void volume than solid volume, giving **e > 1** — which is common in soft organic clays. Porosity, whose denominator includes the voids themselves, is necessarily a fraction less than one.

**The conversions:**

> **e = n/(1 − n)**  and  **n = e/(1 + e)**

Option (c) is the **degree of saturation S**, and option (d) is the **air content**.

**Typical values:**

| Soil | Void ratio |
|---|---|
| Dense sand | 0.4 – 0.5 |
| Loose sand | 0.7 – 0.9 |
| Stiff clay | 0.6 – 1.0 |
| **Soft clay** | **1.0 – 2.0** |
| Organic clay, peat | up to 15 |

**Why e rather than n is used** in most soil mechanics relations: the **volume of solids does not change** as the soil compresses, so e changes only through its numerator. That makes it the natural variable for consolidation, where the whole analysis tracks the change in void ratio against effective stress — the e–log σ′ curve.

examTip.trap: **Porosity** is the near-miss and the two are constantly swapped. Porosity is voids over **TOTAL** volume; void ratio is voids over **SOLIDS**.
examTip.trick: Void ratio can exceed 1 (a soft clay may be at e = 1.5); porosity never can, since it is a fraction of the whole. If an option allows a value above 1, it is the void ratio.
examTip.mnemonic: **e = V_v/V_s, n = V_v/V.** Convert with **e = n/(1−n)** and **n = e/(1+e)**.

questions.stem: The fundamental relation connecting void ratio, degree of saturation, water content and specific gravity is:
questions.solution:
**e·S = w·G.**

This single relation, with the definitions of the phase ratios, answers virtually every phase-relation problem set in the examination — and it is worth deriving once so it can be reconstructed rather than merely recalled.

**Derivation.** Take the volume of solids as unity, so V_s = 1 and V_v = e.

> Volume of water **V_w = S · V_v = S e**
> Weight of water **W_w = S e γ_w**
> Weight of solids **W_s = G γ_w** (since V_s = 1)
> Water content **w = W_w/W_s = S e γ_w /(G γ_w) = S e / G**

Rearranging gives **e S = w G**. ∎

**The special case worth memorising:**

> For a **fully saturated** soil, **S = 1**, so **e = w G**

which is how the void ratio of a saturated clay is found from a simple water content test — no volume measurement needed.

**A worked check.** A saturated clay with w = 40% and G = 2.70: **e = 0.40 × 2.70 = 1.08**. A void ratio slightly above 1 is entirely reasonable for a soft saturated clay, which confirms the arithmetic.

**Everything else follows from it**, combined with the unit weight expressions:

> **γ = (G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e)** · **γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + e)** · **γ_sat = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e)** · **γ′ = (G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)**

Each is obtained by writing the total weight over the total volume for the appropriate condition — again with V_s taken as unity.

examTip.trick: This one relation solves most phase problems. Check it at saturation: with **S = 1** it reduces to **e = wG**, which is the standard saturated-soil shortcut.
examTip.mnemonic: **"See Sw-GEE" — eS = wG.** Learn this and the whole phase diagram opens up; almost every other relation can be derived from it plus the definitions.

questions.stem: The submerged (effective) unit weight of a soil is given by:
questions.solution:
**γ′ = (G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e).**

It follows directly from **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w**:

> γ′ = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e) − γ_w = [(G + e) − (1 + e)]γ_w/(1 + e) = **(G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)** ∎

**The four unit weights, and each option here is one of them:**

| Unit weight | Expression | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| **Bulk (moist)** | **(G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e)** | Any degree of saturation |
| **Dry** | **Gγ_w/(1 + e)** | S = 0 (no water weight) |
| **Saturated** | **(G + e)γ_w/(1 + e)** | S = 1 |
| **Submerged (effective)** | **(G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)** | Below the water table |

Notice that the **bulk** expression reduces to the **dry** value at S = 0 and to the **saturated** value at S = 1 — a useful check that the right formula has been recalled.

**Why the submerged unit weight matters.** Below the water table, the soil is **buoyed up** by the water it displaces, so the **effective** weight causing stress on the soil skeleton is reduced. Computing effective stress below the water table is therefore done in either of two equivalent ways:

> **σ′ = σ − u** (total stress minus pore pressure), **or**
> **σ′ = Σ(γ′ × thickness)** directly, using the submerged unit weight below the water table

The second route is quicker, and the fact that both give the same answer is itself a check on the arithmetic.

**A useful approximation:** for G = 2.65 and a typical e, **γ′ ≈ γ_sat/2 ≈ 9–10 kN/m³**. That is why **a rising water table roughly halves the effective stress** contributed by the submerged soil — and hence roughly halves the frictional component of shear strength, which is the quantitative reason monsoon seepage triggers so many slope failures.

examTip.trap: (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e) is the deliberate distractor — that is the **saturated** unit weight. Submerged is that minus γ_w.
examTip.trick: Derive rather than memorise: **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = (G + e)γ_w/(1+e) − γ_w = (G − 1)γ_w/(1+e)** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Submerged has G − 1 on top; saturated has G + e.** γ′ is roughly **half** of γ_sat for ordinary soils, which is a useful order-of-magnitude check.

questions.stem: In the Casagrande apparatus, the liquid limit is the water content corresponding to a groove closure at:
questions.solution:
**25 blows.**

The liquid limit is the water content at which the two halves of a soil pat, separated by a standard groove, **close over a length of 12 mm** after exactly **25 blows** of the Casagrande cup falling through **10 mm**.

In practice the test is run at **four or five water contents** giving blow counts between about 15 and 35, and the results plotted as water content against **log(number of blows)** — the **flow curve**, which is a straight line. The liquid limit is then **read off at 25 blows** rather than achieved by trial, which is both quicker and more reliable.

**The slope of that flow curve is the FLOW INDEX I_f**, and it measures how rapidly the soil loses strength as its water content rises.

**The three Atterberg limits**, in **descending** order of water content:

| Limit | Water content at which | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid limit (LL)** | The soil begins to **flow as a liquid** | **Casagrande, 25 blows**; or cone penetrometer, **20 mm in 5 s** |
| **Plastic limit (PL)** | The soil **ceases to be plastic** and crumbles | Rolled into a **3 mm thread** which just crumbles |
| **Shrinkage limit (SL)** | Further drying causes **no further volume reduction** | Mercury displacement |

**The cone penetrometer method** is now often preferred to the Casagrande cup because it is **less operator-dependent** — the Casagrande result varies with the operator's rate of turning, the hardness of the base, and the exact groove shape, whereas the cone simply falls under gravity.

**Why 25 blows and 12 mm?** They are **conventions**, chosen by Casagrande to give a repeatable value near the true liquid state. Like the 5-day BOD test, the numbers have no physical significance beyond the agreement to use them — which is why the apparatus, the base hardness and the drop height are all specified precisely.

examTip.trick: The full specification matters: a **13 mm groove closure at 25 blows**, with the cup falling **10 mm** each time. Since hitting exactly 25 is luck, the test is run at several water contents and the value read off the **flow curve** at 25.
examTip.mnemonic: **25 blows, 13 mm closure.** The plastic limit is the quite different 3 mm thread test.

questions.stem: Cavitation in a hydraulic system occurs when the local pressure falls to:
options: The vapour pressure of the liquid
questions.solution:
**The VAPOUR PRESSURE of the liquid at the prevailing temperature.**

**The mechanism:**

> Where the local pressure falls to the **vapour pressure**, the liquid **BOILS at ambient temperature**, forming **vapour bubbles**. Carried into a region of higher pressure, these bubbles **COLLAPSE VIOLENTLY** — and the collapse is what does the damage.

**Vapour pressure of water:**

| Temperature | Vapour pressure |
|---|---|
| **20 °C** | **2.34 kPa** (0.24 m of water) |
| 40 °C | 7.4 kPa |
| 60 °C | 19.9 kPa |
| **100 °C** | **101.3 kPa** — which is why water boils at 100 °C at sea level |

> Note the last line: **boiling is simply the condition vapour pressure = ambient pressure.** Water boils at 100 °C because that is where its vapour pressure reaches one atmosphere — and at altitude, where the atmospheric pressure is lower, **it boils cooler**. On a Himalayan pass at 5000 m, water boils at about **83 °C**.

**Why the collapse is so damaging:**

| Effect | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| Local pressure at collapse | Up to **1000 MPa** in a microjet |
| **Pitting and erosion** of metal surfaces | Pits the hardest steels |
| **Noise** — a characteristic gravel-in-the-pipe rattle | The audible warning |
| **Vibration** | — |
| **Loss of efficiency** and head | The vapour occupies volume that should carry water |

**Where cavitation occurs:**

| Location | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Pump SUCTION side** | The lowest pressure in the system |
| **Impeller and turbine runner blades** | High local velocity → low pressure by Bernoulli |
| **Downstream of a partly closed valve** | Vena contracta |
| **Spillways** — at surface irregularities and on steep chutes | Very high velocity |
| Venturi throat | The point of minimum pressure |
| Draft tube of a reaction turbine | — |

**Preventing it in a PUMP** — the governing quantity is **NPSH**:

> **NPSH_available = (p_atm − p_vapour)/γ − h_suction − h_losses**
> Required: **NPSH_available > NPSH_required** (a property of the pump, from its manufacturer)

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **REDUCE the suction lift** — place the pump **LOWER**, ideally below the water level | The single most effective measure |
| **Shorten and enlarge the suction pipe**; minimise fittings | Reduces h_losses |
| Reduce the pumped liquid's temperature | Lowers p_vapour |
| Choose a pump with a lower NPSH_required | — |
| Avoid throttling on the suction side | Never throttle a suction line |

**Placing the pump below the water level (a flooded suction) eliminates the problem entirely** by making the suction head positive, and it is the standard solution wherever the site permits.

**A note for Nepal**: at altitude the **atmospheric pressure is lower**, so **NPSH_available is reduced** — roughly 1.1 m of water head less for every 1000 m of elevation. A pump installation that works at Terai elevations may cavitate at Kathmandu's 1400 m, and one designed for Kathmandu may fail at 3000 m. Pump selection must use the **site's atmospheric pressure**, not the sea-level value.

**On SPILLWAYS**, cavitation is prevented by **AERATION**: an aerator ramp entrains air into the flow, and the compressible air cushions the bubble collapse. Surface irregularities are also strictly limited — an offset of a few millimetres into a 30 m/s flow is enough to initiate cavitation damage.

examTip.trap: "Atmospheric pressure" is the intuitive wrong answer — but a liquid boils when its pressure reaches its **vapour** pressure, which at 20 °C is only 2.34 kPa.
examTip.trick: Boiling is simply p = p_vapour. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level because that is where its vapour pressure reaches one atmosphere — and at **83 °C on a 5000 m pass**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cavitation calculations must be done in ABSOLUTE pressure.** And in Nepal, subtract for altitude: NPSH available falls about **1.1 m per 1000 m** of elevation, so a pump that works in the Terai may cavitate in Kathmandu.

questions.stem: Fresh concrete, drilling mud and toothpaste behave as:
options: Bingham plastics, requiring a yield stress before flow begins
questions.solution:
**Bingham plastics — they require a YIELD STRESS before flow begins.**

> **τ = τ_y + μ_p (du/dy)** — no flow at all until **τ exceeds τ_y**

**The classification of fluids by their τ – du/dy relationship:**

| Type | Relationship | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Ideal** | **τ = 0** always; μ = 0 | Hypothetical; a useful idealisation |
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ = μ(du/dy)** — straight line **through the origin** | **Water, air, most oils** |
| **Dilatant** (shear-thickening) | τ = k(du/dy)ⁿ, **n > 1** | Starch suspension, **wet sand** |
| **Pseudoplastic** (shear-thinning) | τ = k(du/dy)ⁿ, **n < 1** | **Paint, blood**, polymer solutions |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC** | **τ = τ_y + μ_p(du/dy)** — an **intercept** on the τ axis | **Fresh CONCRETE, drilling mud, toothpaste, sewage sludge** |
| Thixotropic | Viscosity **decreases with TIME** under shear | Some gels, **sensitive clays** |
| Rheopectic | Viscosity increases with time under shear | Rare |

**Why the yield stress matters practically** — for fresh concrete it explains almost everything about its handling:

| Observation | Explained by |
|---|---|
| Concrete **holds its shape** after the slump cone is lifted | Below τ_y, it does not flow |
| It can be placed on a **slope** without running off | Same |
| **VIBRATION** makes it flow into the formwork | Vibration **temporarily reduces τ_y** to near zero |
| **Over-vibration causes SEGREGATION** | With τ_y removed, the heavy aggregate **sinks** through the paste |
| The **slump test** measures something meaningful | Slump correlates with the yield stress |
| Self-compacting concrete needs no vibration | It is formulated with a **very low τ_y** |

**Vibration is the engineering exploitation of the yield stress**: it converts a material that will not flow into one that will, for exactly as long as the vibrator runs, then lets it stiffen again in place. But because it removes the very property that holds the aggregate in suspension, **over-vibration segregates the mix** — which is why vibration is specified by duration and spacing rather than applied until the concrete looks convenient.

**Paint is the pseudoplastic example worth carrying**, because it shows why shear-thinning is useful:

> Paint is **thin under the brush** (high shear rate — it spreads easily) and **thick on the wall** (low shear rate — it does not run). A Newtonian paint of the same average viscosity would either be hard to brush or would sag.

**Thixotropy** deserves separate note because it appears in soil mechanics:

> A **sensitive clay** remoulded by pile driving loses much of its strength, then **regains it with time at constant water content**. That is thixotropy, and it is why a driven pile's capacity **increases over days or weeks** — the **set-up** effect — and why a pile load test done too soon understates the capacity.

**The distinction between thixotropic and shear-thinning** is the variable: **pseudoplastic** viscosity depends on the **shear RATE**; **thixotropic** viscosity depends on the **TIME** for which shear has been applied, and recovers when shearing stops.

examTip.trick: A Bingham plastic will not move at all until the stress exceeds **τ_y** — which is why concrete holds its shape after the slump cone lifts and can be placed on a slope.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vibration temporarily destroys the yield stress** — that is exactly how a poker works. And it is why **over-vibration segregates**: remove τ_y and the heavy aggregate sinks through the paste.

questions.stem: The kinematic viscosity of a fluid is:
options: The product of dynamic viscosity and density
The same as the dynamic viscosity
The ratio of density to dynamic viscosity
The ratio of dynamic viscosity to density, μ/ρ
questions.solution:
**ν = μ/ρ**, the ratio of dynamic viscosity to density.

| | **Dynamic viscosity μ** | **Kinematic viscosity ν** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | From **τ = μ du/dy** | **μ/ρ** |
| **SI unit** | **Pa·s** = N·s/m² | **m²/s** |
| **CGS unit** | **poise** (1 Pa·s = 10 P) | **stokes** (1 m²/s = 10⁴ St) |
| **Water at 20 °C** | **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** | **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s** |
| **Air at 20 °C** | 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s | **1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s** |
| Governs | The **shear STRESS** | The **DIFFUSION of momentum** |

**Note the striking comparison between air and water:**

> Air is about **55 times LESS viscous than water in DYNAMIC terms**, but about **15 times MORE viscous in KINEMATIC terms** — because its density is 800 times lower.

That is not a contradiction but a reminder that the two viscosities answer different questions. **Dynamic** viscosity tells you the shear stress for a given velocity gradient. **Kinematic** viscosity tells you how fast momentum **diffuses** through the fluid — and it is the quantity that appears in the **Reynolds number**:

> **Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν**

**Why ν has units of m²/s** — the same as a diffusion coefficient or a thermal diffusivity — is the physical clue: **kinematic viscosity IS the diffusivity of momentum**, exactly as thermal diffusivity α = k/(ρc) is the diffusivity of heat. A fluid with high ν spreads a velocity disturbance quickly through itself.

**Which one to use:**

| Problem | Use |
|---|---|
| Shear force on a plate, torque in a bearing | **μ** (dynamic) |
| **Reynolds number**, boundary layer thickness | **ν** (kinematic) |
| Head loss in laminar pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille) | Either — **h_f = 32μVL/(γD²) = 32νVL/(gD²)** |
| Terminal velocity, Stokes' law | **μ** |

**Measurement.** Kinematic viscosity is what most viscometers actually measure, because they time the flow of a fixed volume of liquid under gravity — and gravity-driven flow depends on μ/ρ:

| Instrument | Principle |
|---|---|
| **Capillary tube (Ostwald, Cannon–Fenske)** | Time for a volume to drain through a capillary; **Hagen–Poiseuille** |
| **Saybolt / Redwood / Engler** | Time for 60 ml to drain through a standard orifice — an empirical scale |
| **Rotating cylinder** | Torque on an inner cylinder in a rotating outer one — measures **μ** directly |
| **Falling sphere** | **Stokes' law**: μ = (γ_s − γ_f)d²/(18V) — good for very viscous liquids |

**The falling-sphere method is the one with the neat derivation**: at terminal velocity the drag balances the submerged weight, and Stokes' drag 3πμVd applies for Re < 1. It is the same relation used in the **hydrometer analysis** of soil grain size — which is a nice cross-connection between fluid mechanics and soil mechanics.

examTip.trick: Check the units: **Pa·s ÷ kg/m³ = m²/s** ✓ — the units of a diffusivity, because ν IS the diffusivity of momentum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Air is 55× less viscous than water in DYNAMIC terms but 15× MORE in KINEMATIC terms**, because its density is 800× lower. Use **μ** for shear force, **ν** for Reynolds number.

questions.stem: An ideal fluid is one which is:
questions.solution:
**Inviscid (μ = 0) and incompressible.**

**An ideal fluid does not exist** — it is an **idealisation**, and a very useful one. Its properties:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Viscosity μ** | **ZERO** — no shear stress, ever |
| **Density** | **Constant** — incompressible |
| **Surface tension** | Zero |
| Shear stress | **None**, even in motion |
| At a boundary | **SLIPS freely** — no no-slip condition |

**Why the idealisation is useful:**

| Benefit | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Bernoulli's equation** applies exactly | No friction loss term needed |
| **Potential flow theory** becomes available | The flow is **irrotational**, and powerful mathematics follows |
| Flow **outside the boundary layer** is well modelled by it | Viscous effects are confined to a thin layer near surfaces |
| Pressure distributions can be computed analytically | For aerofoils, weirs, bends |

**The essential insight — Prandtl's boundary layer concept:**

> In a **real** fluid of low viscosity, the viscous effects are **confined to a THIN LAYER near solid boundaries** (the boundary layer). **Outside** that layer the flow behaves very nearly as an **ideal fluid**.

That division is what makes practical fluid mechanics possible: solve the **outer** flow by ideal (potential) theory, and the **thin boundary layer** by viscous theory, then match them. Before Prandtl (1904), the two branches of the subject — mathematical hydrodynamics, which predicted no drag at all, and practical hydraulics, which measured plenty — could not be reconciled.

**D'Alembert's paradox** is the classic illustration of the idealisation's limit:

> Ideal flow theory predicts **ZERO DRAG** on any body moving steadily through an ideal fluid — because the pressure distribution is perfectly symmetric fore and aft.

Real bodies obviously experience drag. The resolution is that **real flow SEPARATES** from the rear of a bluff body, destroying the pressure recovery and leaving a low-pressure wake — a phenomenon that has no counterpart in ideal flow, and which accounts for most of the drag on a bluff body.

**Real fluid effects that an ideal fluid cannot represent:**

| Effect | Requires |
|---|---|
| **Head loss / friction** in pipes | Viscosity |
| **Drag** on bodies | Viscosity, separation |
| **Boundary layer** | Viscosity and no-slip |
| **Separation and wake** | Viscosity |
| **Turbulence** | Viscosity (for its dissipation) |
| **Water hammer** wave speed | Compressibility |

**Where ideal fluid analysis is nevertheless used successfully:**

| Application | Why it works |
|---|---|
| Flow through **short converging** sections — nozzles, venturi throats, orifices | **Accelerating** flow has a **thin** boundary layer and **no separation** |
| **Flow over a weir** or through a sluice | Short, accelerating |
| Wave motion | Viscosity negligible over the wave scale |
| Pressure distribution on a **streamlined** body | Boundary layer stays attached |

**Note the pattern in the first row**: ideal flow works well in **accelerating (converging)** flow and poorly in **decelerating (diverging)** flow — because an **adverse pressure gradient** thickens the boundary layer and causes **separation**. That is why a venturi's converging cone can be short and steep (20°) while its diverging cone must be long and gentle (5–7°): the converging flow is well behaved, the diverging flow is on the edge of separating.

examTip.trick: Ideal means **no viscosity and constant density** — so no shear stress ever, no boundary layer, and free slip at a wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **No viscosity, no drag — which is D'Alembert's paradox**, resolved only by real flow SEPARATING. Ideal theory works well in **accelerating (converging)** flow and badly in **decelerating (diverging)** flow — hence a venturi's steep 20° inlet and gentle 6° outlet.

questions.stem: The specific weight of water at 4 °C in SI units is:
questions.solution:
**9810 N/m³**, or **9.81 kN/m³**.

> **γ = ρg = 1000 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² = 9810 N/m³**

**The four related properties, kept distinct** — and confusing them is the commonest source of error in fluid mechanics arithmetic:

| Property | Symbol | Definition | Water at 4 °C | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Density** | **ρ** | **Mass** per unit volume | **1000** | **kg/m³** |
| **Specific weight** (unit weight) | **γ** | **WEIGHT** per unit volume = **ρg** | **9810** | **N/m³** |
| **Specific gravity** (relative density) | **S** or G | Ratio to water — **DIMENSIONLESS** | **1.0** | — |
| **Specific volume** | **v** | Volume per unit mass = **1/ρ** | **0.001** | **m³/kg** |

**Density is mass-based; specific weight is force-based.** The distinction matters because pressure is a force per area:

> **p = γh** — uses the **specific weight**, giving N/m² directly
> **p = ρgh** — the same thing written out

Using ρ where γ belongs gives an answer **9.81 times too small**, and it is a very common slip.

**Water's density anomaly** is worth knowing, and it is why the question specifies 4 °C:

> **Water is DENSEST at 4 °C**, not at 0 °C. Below 4 °C it **expands** as it cools, and **ice is LESS dense than water** — which is why ice floats.

| Temperature | Density (kg/m³) |
|---|---|
| 0 °C (ice) | **917** |
| 0 °C (water) | 999.8 |
| **4 °C** | **1000.0 — maximum** |
| 20 °C | 998.2 |
| 100 °C | 958.4 |

**The consequences of that anomaly are considerable:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Lakes freeze from the TOP down** | The 4 °C water sinks; the colder water stays on top and freezes there, insulating the depths — so **aquatic life survives the winter** |
| **Frost damage to concrete and rock** | Water expands about **9% on freezing**, and the pressure **cracks** the material |
| Frost heave | Ice lenses grow and lift the ground |
| Burst pipes | The same expansion |

**Specific gravity** is dimensionless and therefore the same in every unit system, which is why soil and rock properties are usually tabulated that way:

| Material | S |
|---|---|
| **Water** | **1.0** |
| **Mercury** | **13.6** |
| Oil | 0.8 – 0.9 |
| **Soil solids (G_s)** | **2.65 – 2.75** |
| Concrete | 2.4 |
| Steel | 7.85 |

**For any fluid: γ = S × 9810 N/m³.** So mercury's specific weight is 13.6 × 9810 = **133 400 N/m³**, which is why a mercury manometer measures a large pressure with a short column — a metre of mercury being worth 13.6 m of water.

**A note on g**: taking **g = 9.81 m/s²** is standard, and the variation over the earth's surface (9.78 at the equator to 9.83 at the poles) is well below the precision of any hydraulic calculation. Some texts use 9.807 or simply 9.8; the difference never matters.

examTip.trap: 1000 is the **density in kg/m³**, not the specific weight. Mixing ρ and γ gives an answer 9.81 times out, and it is the single commonest arithmetic error in hydrostatics.
examTip.trick: **γ = ρg = 1000 × 9.81 = 9810 N/m³.** Pressure is a force per area, so it needs γ, not ρ: **p = γh**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water is densest at 4 °C, not 0 °C** — which is why lakes freeze from the top down and why ice (917 kg/m³) floats.

questions.stem: The no-slip condition at a solid boundary means that:
options: The fluid slides freely over the surface
The pressure is zero at the surface
The shear stress is zero at the surface
The fluid velocity relative to the boundary is zero
questions.solution:
**The fluid velocity RELATIVE to the boundary is zero** — the fluid adheres to the surface.

**It is an experimental fact, not a derived result**, and it holds for every real (viscous) fluid on every solid surface. An **ideal** fluid, having no viscosity, would slip freely — which is one of the ways the idealisation departs from reality.

**Everything about viscous flow follows from it:**

| Consequence | Chain of reasoning |
|---|---|
| A **velocity GRADIENT** must exist near the wall | Velocity goes from 0 at the wall to the free-stream value |
| Hence a **SHEAR STRESS** τ = μ(du/dy) at the wall | The gradient is largest there |
| Hence **DRAG** on every surface | The wall shear integrated over the area |
| Hence **HEAD LOSS** in every pipe | The drag must be overcome by a pressure drop |
| Hence the **BOUNDARY LAYER** | The region over which the velocity adjusts |

> **Without no-slip there would be no friction, no boundary layer, no head loss, and no need for pumps.** The whole practical subject of hydraulics rests on it.

**The everyday demonstration**: dust remains on a fan blade however fast it spins, and a car does not clean itself by driving fast. The air immediately at the surface is **not moving relative to it**, so it exerts no sweeping force on the dust.

**Option (c) is exactly backwards** and worth correcting explicitly: the shear stress at the wall is not zero but is **at its MAXIMUM** there, because the velocity gradient is steepest at the wall. In pipe flow the shear stress varies **linearly** from **τ₀ at the wall to zero at the centreline**:

> **τ = τ₀ (r/R)**, with **τ₀ = (γ h_f D)/(4L) = ρ g R S**

**The velocity profile** correspondingly:

| Flow | Wall shear | Profile |
|---|---|---|
| **Laminar pipe flow** | Maximum at wall | **PARABOLIC**; **V_mean = V_max/2** |
| **Turbulent pipe flow** | Maximum at wall | **Logarithmic** — much **flatter**; **V_mean ≈ 0.82 V_max** |

**The turbulent profile is flatter** because turbulent mixing transports momentum across the section far more effectively than molecular viscosity, evening out the velocity — but it is **steeper right at the wall**, within the thin **viscous sublayer**, which is why turbulent friction is higher.

**The viscous sublayer** is the key to the smooth/rough pipe distinction:

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Roughness **submerged** in the viscous sublayer | Pipe behaves as **HYDRODYNAMICALLY SMOOTH** — f depends on **Re only** |
| Roughness **projecting through** it | **Fully rough** — f depends on **k/D only**, not on Re |
| Between | Transitional — f depends on both (the Colebrook–White region) |

> So **"smooth" and "rough" are not properties of the pipe alone** but of the pipe **and the flow**: the same pipe is smooth at low Reynolds number and rough at high, because the sublayer thins as the flow accelerates. That is why the Moody diagram's curves become horizontal at high Re — the flow has gone fully rough and the Reynolds number no longer matters.

examTip.trap: "Shear stress is zero at the surface" is exactly backwards — the wall is where the shear is **maximum**, because the velocity gradient is steepest there.
examTip.trick: No-slip creates the velocity gradient, which creates the wall shear, which creates the drag and the head loss. Everything in viscous flow follows from it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dust stays on a spinning fan blade.** Shear stress in a pipe varies **linearly from τ₀ at the wall to zero at the centreline** — in both laminar and turbulent flow.

questions.stem: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**8σ/d — twice that of a droplet of the same size.**

**Because a soap bubble has TWO surfaces** — an inner and an outer face of the thin liquid film — each contributing a surface tension force σπd around the circumference:

> Pressure force = **Δp × πd²/4**
> Surface tension force = **2 × σ × πd**
> **Δp = 8σ/d** ✓

**The three cases side by side:**

| Case | Surfaces | Curvature | Δp |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cylindrical JET** | 1 | One direction only | **2σ/d** |
| **Liquid DROPLET** | 1 | Two directions | **4σ/d** |
| **SOAP BUBBLE** | **2** | Two directions | **8σ/d** |

**The pattern is systematic**: each factor of two comes from a distinct cause — the second direction of curvature doubles the jet's value to the droplet's, and the second surface doubles the droplet's to the bubble's.

> The unifying statement is the **Young–Laplace equation**: **Δp = σ(1/R₁ + 1/R₂)** per surface. A cylinder has R₂ = ∞ (2σ/d); a sphere has R₁ = R₂ = d/2 (4σ/d); a bubble is two spherical surfaces (8σ/d).

**A consequence worth knowing**: connect a **small** bubble to a **large** one and the **small one EMPTIES INTO THE LARGE**, because its internal pressure is higher. That is counter-intuitive — one expects them to equalise at an intermediate size — and it explains why a foam **coarsens** over time, small bubbles disappearing into larger ones.

**The same argument applies to alveoli in the lung**, where it would be disastrous — the small alveoli would collapse into the large. Nature's solution is a **surfactant** whose surface tension **falls as the surface contracts**, stabilising the small alveoli. It is a nice illustration that the physics is real enough to have driven a biological adaptation.

**Surface tension values and influences:**

| Factor | Effect on σ |
|---|---|
| **Temperature increase** | **DECREASES** — reaching zero at the critical point |
| **Detergent / surfactant** | **DECREASES sharply** — the mechanism by which detergents work |
| Dissolved salts | Slight increase |
| Contamination | Usually decreases |

**Water at 20 °C: σ = 0.073 N/m.** Mercury, at 0.51 N/m, is much higher — which is why mercury beads up so tightly.

**Where surface tension matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Capillary rise** in soils and fine tubes | **h = 4σcos θ/(γd)** |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | Menisci bind the grains |
| **Manometer** readings in fine-bore tubes | A capillary correction is needed — which is why manometer tubes are specified at 6 mm or more |
| **Weir flow at very low heads** | Surface tension distorts the nappe, so weir formulae specify a **minimum head** (typically 30 mm) |
| Droplet formation in sprinklers and aerators | — |
| Flotation of fine particles | — |

**The weir point is a practical one**: below about 30 mm head the nappe clings to the weir plate and the discharge coefficient departs from its tabulated value — so a weir cannot be used to measure very small flows accurately, and a V-notch (which concentrates a small flow into a greater head) is used instead.

examTip.trick: A bubble is a **film with two surfaces**, inner and outer, so the surface tension force is doubled: **8σ/d** against the droplet's 4σ/d.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two surfaces, twice the pressure.** Consequence: connect a small bubble to a large one and the **small one empties into the large**, because its pressure is higher. That is why foam coarsens over time.

questions.stem: An oil has specific gravity 0.8 and dynamic viscosity 0.04 Pa·s. Its kinematic viscosity is:
questions.solution:
**5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s.**

> **ρ = S × ρ_water = 0.8 × 1000 = 800 kg/m³**
> **ν = μ/ρ = 0.04 / 800 = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s**

**The trap in this question** is option (a), 0.032 — which is **μ × S**, or equivalently what you get by **multiplying instead of dividing**, and by using the specific gravity in place of the density. Two errors that happen to combine into a plausible-looking number.

**Check the units**, which settles it immediately:

> **μ/ρ = (Pa·s)/(kg/m³) = (N·s/m²)/(kg/m³) = (kg·m/s²·s/m²)/(kg/m³) = m²/s** ✓

And the magnitude is a further check: **oil is more viscous than water**, whose ν is 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s — so an answer of 5 × 10⁻⁵ (fifty times water's) is sensible for a light oil, while 0.032 m²/s would be **32 000 times** water's, which is the viscosity of a heavy grease.

**Developing a feel for the magnitudes** is worth the effort, because it catches errors that unit checks do not:

| Fluid | ν (m²/s) | Relative to water |
|---|---|---|
| **Water (20 °C)** | **1.0 × 10⁻⁶** | **1** |
| **Air (20 °C)** | 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ | 15 |
| Light oil | 5 × 10⁻⁵ | 50 |
| SAE 30 engine oil | 1 × 10⁻⁴ | 100 |
| Glycerine | 1.2 × 10⁻³ | 1200 |
| **Honey** | ~1 × 10⁻² | 10 000 |

**Why kinematic viscosity is the useful one here** — it feeds directly into the Reynolds number:

> **Re = VD/ν**

For this oil flowing at 1 m/s in a 50 mm pipe:

> **Re = 1 × 0.05 / (5 × 10⁻⁵) = 1000** — **LAMINAR** (Re < 2000)

Whereas water in the same pipe at the same speed gives **Re = 50 000** — firmly turbulent. That difference of regime changes everything about the flow: the velocity profile, the friction factor, the mixing, and the head loss relationship.

**The head loss comparison makes the point:**

| Regime | Head loss varies as |
|---|---|
| **Laminar** | **h_f ∝ V** — directly with velocity; **f = 64/Re** |
| **Turbulent** | **h_f ∝ V^1.75 to V²** |

So doubling the flow in the oil pipe doubles the head loss; doubling it in the water pipe roughly quadruples it. **Oil pipelines are laminar and water pipelines turbulent**, which is why they are analysed with different tools and why the friction factor for an oil line depends only on Re, not on the pipe roughness at all.

**A word on the CGS units**, still met in oil specifications: **1 stokes = 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s**, and **1 centistokes = 10⁻⁶ m²/s** — which happens to be exactly the kinematic viscosity of water at 20 °C. So a viscosity quoted in **centistokes is a direct multiple of water's**, which is a convenient scale and the reason it persists.

examTip.trap: 0.032 is what you get by **multiplying** by the specific gravity instead of dividing by the density — two errors that combine into a plausible-looking number.
examTip.trick: **ρ = 0.8 × 1000 = 800; ν = 0.04/800 = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s.** Sanity check the magnitude: water is 1 × 10⁻⁶, so a light oil at 50× water is sensible; 0.032 would be 32 000× water — a heavy grease.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always sanity-check ν against water's 10⁻⁶.**

questions.stem: A fluid at rest cannot sustain:
questions.solution:
**Shear stress.**

**This follows directly from the definition of a fluid:**

> A fluid **deforms continuously under ANY shear stress, however small**. So if a shear stress existed in a fluid at rest, the fluid would **flow** — and it would no longer be at rest. The two conditions are incompatible.

**Therefore in a static fluid the only stress is the NORMAL stress**, which is the **pressure** — and that leads immediately to the foundational result of hydrostatics:

> **PASCAL'S LAW: the pressure at a point in a fluid at rest is the SAME IN ALL DIRECTIONS.**

**Why Pascal's law follows.** Consider a small wedge-shaped element of fluid at rest. With no shear stresses on any face, only the normal (pressure) forces act. Resolving in two directions and letting the element shrink to a point, the weight term (proportional to volume) vanishes faster than the pressure terms (proportional to area) — and the pressures on all faces are found to be **equal**, whatever the orientation of the wedge.

**The consequences are the whole of hydrostatics:**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| Pressure acts **PERPENDICULAR** to any surface | Because there is no shear component |
| **p = γh** — pressure increases **linearly** with depth | From the equilibrium of a vertical column |
| Pressure is the **same at all points on a horizontal plane** in a connected fluid | The basis of the **manometer** and of communicating vessels |
| **Hydrostatic paradox** | The force on a base depends on the **DEPTH and AREA only** — not on the shape of the vessel or the weight of liquid it holds |
| Pascal's principle of transmission | An applied pressure is transmitted **undiminished** throughout — the **hydraulic jack** |

**The hydrostatic paradox deserves its name** and is worth stating because it surprises people every time:

> Three vessels — one cylindrical, one flaring outward, one narrowing to a thin neck — with the **same base area** and the **same depth of water** exert **exactly the same force on the base**, even though they contain **utterly different weights of water**.

The resolution is that the **walls** carry the difference: in the flaring vessel the walls push down on the liquid, in the narrowing one they push up. The base force depends only on **p = γh** and the area.

**Options (b), (c) and (d) are all things a static fluid CAN sustain**, and each is worth a word:

| Option | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| **Normal stress** | A static fluid sustains it perfectly well — that **is** the pressure |
| **Pressure** | Same |
| **Its own weight** | It sustains it; the weight is precisely what **creates** the pressure variation with depth, p = γh |

**A refinement worth noting**: a fluid at rest cannot sustain shear, but it **can sustain TENSION** in principle — water can be put under a small negative absolute pressure in very clean, carefully prepared conditions. In practice **cavitation intervenes** at the vapour pressure, so for engineering purposes the absolute pressure in a liquid cannot fall below its vapour pressure, and negative gauge pressures are limited to about −10 m of water.

**And for a fluid IN MOTION**, shear stresses do exist — τ = μ(du/dy) — so the pressure at a point is no longer strictly equal in all directions. In practice the differences are tiny for ordinary flows, and the **mean** of the three normal stresses is what is called the pressure.

examTip.trick: If a fluid at rest could sustain shear it would flow, and then it would not be at rest. The two conditions are incompatible.
examTip.mnemonic: **No shear at rest → pressure acts EQUALLY IN ALL DIRECTIONS (Pascal) and PERPENDICULAR to every surface.** From that single fact follow p = γh, the manometer, and the hydrostatic paradox.

questions.stem: A liquid is generally regarded as incompressible in civil engineering because:
options: Its bulk modulus is very large, so the volume change under working pressures is negligible
questions.solution:
**Because its bulk modulus is very large, so the volume change under ordinary working pressures is negligible.**

> **K_water = 2.1 GPa.** A pressure of **1 MPa (about 100 m of head)** compresses water by **1/2100 ≈ 0.05%**.

That is far below the accuracy of any hydraulic calculation, so treating the density as constant introduces no meaningful error.

**The simplification is enormous**, and it is worth seeing what it buys:

| Simplification | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **ρ constant** | Continuity becomes **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂** — a simple volumetric statement |
| Bernoulli in **head** form | **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant** — every term a length |
| No thermodynamic coupling | Temperature and pressure need not be solved together |
| **Free surface** problems tractable | Open channel flow, weirs, reservoirs |

**But there are situations where the compressibility of water is essential**, and they are examinable:

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER** | The pressure wave travels at **c = √(K/ρ) = 1440 m/s**. Treat water as truly incompressible and the wave speed is **infinite** and the pressure rise **unbounded** — the analysis fails completely |
| Underwater acoustics, sonar | Sound is a compression wave |
| Very deep ocean | Density increases measurably with depth |
| Hydraulic transients generally | Surge analysis |

**Water hammer** is the one that matters in practice:

> **Joukowsky: Δp = ρ c ΔV.** Water at 2 m/s stopped instantly gives **Δp = 1000 × 1440 × 2 = 2.88 MPa ≈ 288 m of head** — enough to burst a pipe designed for 100 m.

**And when is a GAS incompressible?** The criterion is the **Mach number**:

> **M = V/c**, and a gas flow may be treated as **incompressible when M < 0.3** — for which the density change is under about 5%.

For air (c ≈ 340 m/s) that means velocities **below about 100 m/s**, which covers essentially all civil engineering: wind loading (design wind speeds up to 55 m/s), ventilation, and air in ducts. So **air is treated as incompressible in civil engineering too**, despite being a gas — which surprises candidates who assume the distinction is between liquids and gases.

> The distinction is **not liquid versus gas** but **whether the density changes appreciably in the flow**. A liquid essentially never does; a gas does only at high speed.

**Where compressible flow does matter**: gas pipelines over long distances (where the pressure drop is large enough to change the density substantially), compressed air systems, and high-speed aerodynamics — none of them core civil engineering, but the gas pipeline case does arise.

**A cautionary note about the word "incompressible"**: it describes an **assumption about the flow**, not an absolute property of the fluid. Water is not literally incompressible — as water hammer proves conclusively — and the assumption must be dropped whenever the phenomenon of interest depends on the compressibility itself.

examTip.trick: 1 MPa (100 m of head) compresses water by **0.05%** — far below the precision of any hydraulic calculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Incompressible describes the FLOW, not the fluid.** Drop the assumption for **water hammer** and acoustics. And note **air is treated as incompressible too** below M = 0.3 (about 100 m/s), which covers all civil engineering wind loading.

questions.stem: The locus of reaction of a two hinged semi - circular arch:
questions.solution:
**straight line.** The locus of reaction of a two hinged semi - circular arch is straight line.

This is a recall item from the NEC revision syllabus: the statement is the whole of it, and the other options are real terms from the same chapter, which is exactly why they look plausible.

examTip.trap: The distractors here are genuine terms from this chapter, so none of them looks obviously wrong — you have to know the specific fact rather than eliminate on sight.
examTip.trick: Fix the whole statement in memory, not the answer alone: "The locus of reaction of a two hinged semi - circular arch is straight line."
examTip.mnemonic: The locus of reaction → straight line

questions.stem: At a section of a beam where the shear force is zero and changes sign, the bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**A maximum or minimum.**

**Because shear force is the DERIVATIVE of bending moment:**

> **V = dM/dx**

so where **V = 0**, **dM/dx = 0** — a stationary point of the bending moment diagram. If V also **changes sign** there, it is a genuine **maximum or minimum**.

**The full set of differential relations**, which govern every shear force and bending moment diagram:

> **w = −dV/dx**  (load intensity)
> **V = dM/dx**  (shear force)

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Slope of the SFD** at a point | **= −load intensity** there |
| **Slope of the BMD** at a point | **= shear force** there |
| **Change in V** between two points | **= −area of the load diagram** between them |
| **Change in M** between two points | **= AREA of the SHEAR diagram** between them |

**The area rule is the fastest way to draw a BMD by hand**, and it should be the default method: compute the shear diagram first, then accumulate its areas.

**The degree relationship** follows from the same integrations, and it is worth knowing because it tells you the shape of each diagram before you draw it:

| Loading | Load | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | — | **Constant** (jumps at the load) | **Linear** |
| **Uniformly distributed** | Constant | **Linear** | **Parabolic** |
| **Triangular (linearly varying)** | Linear | **Parabolic** | **Cubic** |
| Couple applied | — | No change | **Jumps** by the couple |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one.** A UDL gives a linear shear and a parabolic moment; that single fact resolves most diagram-shape questions.

**Discontinuities:**

| At a | Shear diagram | Moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Point LOAD** | **JUMPS** by the load | **Kink** (slope changes) — but continuous |
| **Applied COUPLE** | **No change** | **JUMPS** by the couple |
| Support reaction | Jumps by the reaction | Kink |

**The couple case catches people out**: an applied moment produces a **step in the BMD** and **no change at all in the SFD** — the opposite of a point load.

**Standard maximum moments** worth having by heart:

| Beam and loading | Maximum moment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported, central point load W** | **WL/4** |
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **wL²/8** |
| **Cantilever, end point load W** | **WL** (at the fixed end) |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **wL²/2** (at the fixed end) |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL w** | **wL²/12** at supports, **wL²/24** at midspan |
| Propped cantilever, UDL w | wL²/8 at the fixed end |

**Note the fixed-ended beam's advantage**: its maximum moment (wL²/12) is **two thirds** of the simply supported value (wL²/8), and it is distributed between support and span rather than concentrated at midspan. That redistribution is why continuity is structurally valuable — and why a continuous beam is lighter than a series of simply supported ones.

**A point of caution on the question's wording**: V = 0 is necessary but not sufficient for a maximum. Where the shear is zero over a **length** (an unloaded region with no shear), the moment is **constant** there — stationary but not a peak. The sign change is what makes it a true extremum.

examTip.trap: "Zero" is offered because the moment IS zero at a point of contraflexure — but that is where the moment **changes sign**, not where the shear does. Two different sections.
examTip.trick: **V = dM/dx**, so V = 0 is the stationary point of the moment diagram. Add a **sign change** and it is a genuine maximum or minimum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slope of the BMD is the shear; slope of the SFD is minus the load.** Each integration raises the degree by one: point load → constant shear → linear moment; UDL → linear shear → parabolic moment.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w per unit length. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**wL²/8**, occurring at **midspan**.

**Derivation.** By symmetry each reaction is **wL/2**. Taking moments at midspan:

> **M = (wL/2)(L/2) − (wL/2)(L/4) = wL²/4 − wL²/8 = wL²/8** ✓

**Or by the area rule**: the shear varies linearly from +wL/2 at the left support to zero at midspan, so the area of the shear diagram over that half-span is **½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8** ✓ — the change in moment from the support (where M = 0) to midspan.

**The two most-used standard results:**

| Loading on a simply supported span L | Maximum moment | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **UDL w** | **wL²/8** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/4** | **WL³/(48EI)** |

**A useful comparison.** For the **same total load** W = wL:

| | Moment | Deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **As a UDL** | **WL/8** | **5WL³/(384EI)** = WL³/76.8EI |
| **As a central point load** | **WL/4** | **WL³/(48EI)** |
| Ratio (point/UDL) | **2.0** | **1.6** |

> A central point load produces **twice the moment** and **1.6 times the deflection** of the same total load spread uniformly. Concentrating load is structurally expensive, which is why loads are distributed wherever the arrangement permits.

**Other standard maximum moments:**

| Beam | Loading | M_max |
|---|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | End load W | **WL** |
| **Cantilever** | UDL w | **wL²/2** |
| **Fixed both ends** | UDL w | **wL²/12** at supports, wL²/24 at midspan |
| **Fixed both ends** | Central load W | WL/8 at both supports and midspan |
| **Propped cantilever** | UDL w | **wL²/8** at the fixed end |
| Simply supported | Point load W at a from one end | **Wab/L** |

**The Wab/L result** is worth carrying because it generalises the WL/4 case: with a = b = L/2 it gives WL/4 ✓, and it handles any off-centre load directly.

**Note the L² dependence** in every distributed-load case:

> **Doubling the span QUADRUPLES the bending moment** for the same load intensity. That is the dominant fact of beam design, and it is why long spans require disproportionately deep sections — or a different structural system altogether (trusses, arches, cables), which carry load primarily by **axial** action rather than bending.

**And the L⁴ in deflection** is more severe still:

> Doubling the span increases the deflection **sixteenfold** at the same load intensity. For long spans **deflection, not strength, usually governs** — which is why span-to-depth ratio limits (IS 456 gives 20 for simply supported, 26 for continuous) exist as a deemed-to-satisfy check.

**A cross-check on the answer's plausibility**: wL²/8 for a 6 m span carrying 20 kN/m gives **90 kN·m** — a sensible design moment for a beam of that span, and consistent with a section around 300 × 500 mm in reinforced concrete.

examTip.trick: Get it from the **area of the shear diagram**: ½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8. Same answer, and it is a check on the formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **UDL wL²/8, central point load WL/4** — the point load gives **twice** the moment for the same total load. Note **M ∝ L²**: doubling the span quadruples the moment, which is why long spans need a different structural system rather than a deeper beam.

questions.stem: A point of contraflexure in a beam is a section where the:
options: Bending moment changes sign, passing through zero
questions.solution:
**Where the bending moment CHANGES SIGN, passing through zero.**

**Also called the point of inflexion.** At that section:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bending moment** | **ZERO** |
| **Curvature** | **Zero** — and it reverses |
| The beam changes from | **Sagging to hogging**, or the reverse |
| Tension moves from | One face to the other |

**Where they occur:**

| Structure | Points of contraflexure |
|---|---|
| **Overhanging beam** | Between the support and the point of maximum sagging moment |
| **Fixed-ended beam under UDL** | At **0.211L from each end** |
| **Propped cantilever under UDL** | At **0.25L from the propped end** |
| **Continuous beam** | Near each interior support |
| Portal frame column | Near mid-height under lateral load |

**Why they matter practically — three distinct reasons:**

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCEMENT CURTAILMENT** | The moment reverses, so **top steel is needed on one side and bottom steel on the other**. The contraflexure point locates where each can be curtailed |
| **HINGE PLACEMENT** in a hinged (Gerber) beam | A hinge carries no moment, so placing it at a natural contraflexure point makes the structure **determinate without changing its moments** |
| **Effective length** of columns | The distance between contraflexure points is the **effective buckling length** — it behaves as a pin-ended strut |

**The reinforcement point is the everyday one**, and getting it wrong is a real and recurring detailing failure:

> Near a continuous support the beam **HOGS** — tension is at the **TOP** — so the main steel must be in the **top face**. Away from the support it **SAGS** and the steel belongs at the **bottom**. Steel curtailed before the moment has actually reversed leaves a section with tension and no reinforcement to carry it.

IS 456 accordingly requires bars to extend a **development length beyond** the point where they are no longer required by calculation, and at least **d or 12φ** past the theoretical cut-off — a margin precisely because the true contraflexure position shifts with the loading pattern.

**That shifting is the subtlety worth stating:**

> The point of contraflexure **MOVES as the loading pattern changes**. A continuous beam loaded on alternate spans has its contraflexure points in quite different places from one loaded on all spans.

So curtailment must be based on the **envelope** of all load cases, not a single analysis — which is why detailing rules are conservative and why simple codified rules (curtail at 0.15L, 0.25L and so on) are provided for standard cases.

**The effective-length application** is worth a note because it links this topic to columns:

> Between two points of contraflexure a member is, in bending terms, **equivalent to a pin-ended strut** — zero moment at both ends. The distance between them is therefore the **effective length L_e** for buckling.

That is the physical reason behind the effective length factors: a fixed–fixed column has contraflexure points at the quarter points, so **L_e = 0.5L**; a fixed–free (cantilever) column has none within its length and its equivalent pin-ended strut is twice as long, so **L_e = 2L**.

**Distinguishing it from the distractors:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| Shear force maximum | Usually at a support |
| **Deflection maximum** | Where the **SLOPE is zero** — a quite different section |
| **Slope zero** | The point of maximum deflection |
| **Moment zero and reversing** | **Contraflexure** ✓ |

**Note that zero moment alone is not enough** — the moment is zero at the ends of every simply supported beam, and those are not points of contraflexure because the moment does not **reverse** there.

examTip.trap: "Deflection is maximum" describes where the **SLOPE is zero** — an entirely different section. And zero moment alone is not enough: the moment is zero at both ends of every simply supported beam, and those are not contraflexure points.
examTip.trick: The moment must **pass through zero AND reverse**. Sagging becomes hogging, so the tension face swaps.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tension moves from the bottom face to the top** — which is why the contraflexure point governs where **reinforcement can be curtailed**. It also **MOVES with the load pattern**, so curtail on the envelope, never on one analysis.

questions.stem: In the shear force diagram of a beam, an applied couple at a section produces:
options: A jump equal to the couple
No change in the shear force
questions.solution:
**No change in the shear force** — the couple produces a **jump in the BENDING MOMENT diagram** instead.

**The contrast with a point load** is the whole point, and it is a standard examination discriminator:

| Applied at a section | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **POINT LOAD W** | **JUMPS by W** | **Kink** — slope changes, but continuous |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change** | **JUMPS by M** |

**Why.** Consider a short element containing the couple:

> **Vertical equilibrium**: a couple applies **no net vertical force**, so the shear on either side is **unchanged**.
> **Moment equilibrium**: the couple must be balanced, so the bending moment **steps by exactly its magnitude**.

**A point load does the reverse**: it applies a vertical force (so V jumps) but contributes no moment at its own location (so M is continuous, though its slope changes because V has changed).

**The complete table of diagram behaviour:**

| Feature | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| Free end | V = 0 | M = 0 |
| **Simply supported end** | V = reaction | **M = 0** |
| **Fixed end** | V = reaction | **M = fixing moment** |
| Internal **hinge** | — | **M = 0** |
| Point load | **Jump** | Kink |
| **Couple** | **Nothing** | **Jump** |
| UDL | Linear | Parabolic |
| Free (unloaded) span | Constant | Linear |

**The internal hinge condition M = 0** is what makes hinged (Gerber) beams determinate: each hinge supplies one extra equation, so a beam with the right number of hinges can be solved by statics alone.

**Where applied couples actually arise in practice:**

| Situation | Source of the couple |
|---|---|
| A **bracket or cantilever** framing into a beam | The eccentric load is resolved into a force plus a **couple** |
| A column framing eccentrically into a beam | Eccentric axial load |
| **Torsion transferred** from a secondary beam | — |
| Fixed-end moments transferred at a joint | Frame analysis |
| A crane bracket on a column | The classic case |

**The bracket case is the everyday one**, and resolving it correctly is a routine skill:

> A load **P at eccentricity e** from a member's axis is statically equivalent to **P acting on the axis PLUS a couple Pe**. The force enters the shear diagram; the couple steps the moment diagram.

Failing to include the couple — analysing only the transferred force — understates the moment, and it is a genuine and common error in the design of brackets, corbels and eccentric column connections.

**Sign conventions**, which must be stated before any diagram is drawn:

| Convention | Positive |
|---|---|
| **Shear force** | Left portion tends to move **UP** relative to the right |
| **Bending moment** | **SAGGING** — compression on top, tension at the bottom |

> Any consistent convention gives correct answers, but **mixing conventions mid-problem** is a reliable source of sign errors. State it once and hold to it.

**A practical drawing check**: at the far end of any beam, the diagram must **close** — the shear must return to zero (or to the final reaction) and the moment must return to zero at a free or simply supported end. A diagram that does not close indicates an arithmetic error, and checking closure catches most slips before they propagate into a design.

examTip.trap: This is a deliberate discriminator and it catches people every sitting — a **point load** jumps the shear diagram, so candidates assume a couple must jump it too.
examTip.trick: A couple applies **no net vertical force**, so vertical equilibrium leaves the shear unchanged. Moment equilibrium forces the BMD to **step** by the couple.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load: jumps V, kinks M. Couple: nothing to V, jumps M.** Where does a couple come from in practice? A **bracket** — a load P at eccentricity e is P on the axis PLUS a couple Pe. Omitting the couple is a real design error.

questions.stem: A cantilever of length 3 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its whole length. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**54 kN·m**, at the fixed end.

> **M_max = wL²/2 = 12 × 3²/2 = 12 × 9/2 = 54 kN·m** ✓

**Option (a), 18 kN·m**, is **wL²/6**; option (c), 36 kN·m, is **WL/2** using the total load W = 36 kN with the wrong lever arm; option (d), 13.5 kN·m, is **wL²/8** — the simply supported value, applied to a cantilever.

**The physical route** confirms it: the total load is **W = 12 × 3 = 36 kN**, acting at its centroid **1.5 m** from the fixed end:

> **M = 36 × 1.5 = 54 kN·m** ✓

**Cantilever standard results:**

| Loading | M_max (at the fixed end) | δ_max (at the free end) |
|---|---|---|
| **End point load W** | **WL** | **WL³/(3EI)** |
| **UDL w** | **wL²/2** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** |
| Triangular, maximum at the fixed end | wL²/6 | 11wL⁴/(120EI) |
| Couple M at the free end | M (constant throughout) | ML²/(2EI) |

**Comparison with a simply supported beam** of the same span and loading:

| | Cantilever | Simply supported | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M_max under UDL** | **wL²/2** | **wL²/8** | **4×** |
| **δ_max under UDL** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** | **9.6×** |

> A cantilever carries **four times the moment** and **nearly ten times the deflection** of a simply supported beam of the same span and load. Cantilevers are structurally expensive, and their **deflection almost always governs**.

**That is why cantilever span-to-depth limits are so much tighter**: IS 456 gives a basic span/depth of **7 for a cantilever** against **20 for a simply supported** beam — a factor of nearly three in required depth.

**Practical points about cantilevers:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tension is at the TOP** | **Main reinforcement goes in the TOP face** — the single most important detailing fact, and a classic site error |
| **Deflection usually governs** | Not strength |
| The **fixed end must genuinely be fixed** | The backspan must provide the restraining moment, with enough dead load to prevent uplift |
| **No redundancy** | A cantilever is **determinate** — failure at the root is **total collapse**, with no alternative load path |
| Sensitive to **construction loading** | Propping removal sequence matters |

**The lack of redundancy deserves emphasis:**

> A cantilever has **no alternative load path**. A continuous beam that yields at one section redistributes moment to others and gives warning; a cantilever that fails at its root **falls**. Balconies and canopies have collapsed for exactly this reason, usually because the top steel was misplaced to the bottom during construction.

That combination — top steel, no redundancy, and an error that is invisible once the concrete is poured — makes cantilever reinforcement one of the details most worth checking personally before a pour.

**The backspan requirement** is the other common oversight: the fixing moment at the root must be equilibrated by the adjoining span. Where the backspan is short or lightly loaded, the cantilever can **lift the far support**, and the design must either provide sufficient dead load or physically tie the support down.

examTip.trap: 13.5 kN·m is **wL²/8** — the simply supported value applied to a cantilever. It is four times too small.
examTip.trick: Check physically: total load 12 × 3 = 36 kN acting at its centroid **1.5 m** from the support, so M = 36 × 1.5 = 54 kN·m ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Cantilever wL²/2 — FOUR times the simply supported wL²/8, and nearly TEN times the deflection.** And the detailing consequence that matters: **tension is at the TOP, so the main steel goes in the top face.** A cantilever is determinate, so an error at the root means collapse, not cracking.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load, the shear force diagram is:
options: Linear, varying from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other
questions.solution:
**Linear, varying from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other**, passing through zero at midspan.

**Because of the differential relation:**

> **dV/dx = −w**

With **w constant** (a UDL), the slope of the shear diagram is constant — so **V varies LINEARLY**.

**And integrating once more:**

> **dM/dx = V**, and V is linear, so **M is PARABOLIC** ✓ — with its maximum at midspan where V = 0.

**The degree ladder**, which predicts every diagram's shape before it is drawn:

| Loading | Load diagram | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | — | **Constant** | **Linear** |
| **UDL** | **Constant** | **Linear** | **Parabolic** |
| **Triangular** | Linear | **Parabolic** | **Cubic** |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one.** That single rule answers most diagram-shape questions without any calculation.

**Values for the simply supported UDL case:**

| Location | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Left support** | **+wL/2** | **0** |
| Quarter point | +wL/4 | 3wL²/32 |
| **Midspan** | **0** | **wL²/8 — maximum** |
| Three-quarter point | −wL/4 | 3wL²/32 |
| **Right support** | **−wL/2** | **0** |

**The sign change at midspan** is exactly the condition for the moment maximum, as required by V = dM/dx.

**Where each governs the design:**

| Quantity | Maximum at | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| **SHEAR** | **The SUPPORTS** | Shear reinforcement (stirrups), web thickness |
| **MOMENT** | **MIDSPAN** | Main flexural reinforcement, section depth |

> They are maximum at **different sections**, which is the basis of efficient detailing: **stirrups closely spaced near the supports** and widely spaced at midspan; **main bars fully provided at midspan** and curtailed toward the supports.

**A caution about the shear used in design**: IS 456 permits the **critical section for shear** to be taken at a distance **d from the face of the support** rather than at the support itself, where the reaction introduces compression that enhances the shear capacity. Using the support value is conservative but wasteful.

**The area rule as a check:**

> Change in moment = **area of the shear diagram**

From the left support to midspan: **½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8** ✓ — the moment at midspan, since M = 0 at the support. That agreement is a quick verification of any hand-drawn pair of diagrams.

**And the closure check**: over the whole span the shear diagram's area must be **zero** (two equal triangles of opposite sign), which correctly returns the moment to zero at the right support ✓.

**For a cantilever under UDL**, by contrast, the shear is **linear from 0 at the free end to wL at the fixed end** (all of one sign, no zero crossing within the span) and the moment is **parabolic from 0 to wL²/2**. The absence of a sign change is why the cantilever's maximum moment is at its **support** rather than within the span — a useful contrast to hold alongside this case.

examTip.trick: **dV/dx = −w**, and w is constant for a UDL, so the shear must vary **linearly** — from +wL/2 through zero at midspan to −wL/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear peaks at the SUPPORTS, moment at MIDSPAN.** Different sections, which is the whole basis of efficient detailing — stirrups close together near the supports, main bars fully provided at midspan. IS 456 also lets you take the critical shear section at **d from the support face**.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a point load of 40 kN at 3 m from the left support. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**75 kN·m**, under the load.

> **M_max = Wab/L**, with a = 3 m, b = 5 m, L = 8 m
> **= 40 × 3 × 5/8 = 600/8 = 75 kN·m** ✓

**Check by reactions:**

> **R_left = Wb/L = 40 × 5/8 = 25 kN**
> **R_right = Wa/L = 40 × 3/8 = 15 kN** (sum = 40 ✓)
> **M under the load = R_left × a = 25 × 3 = 75 kN·m** ✓

**Both routes agree.** Option (a), 80 kN·m, is **WL/4** — the value for a **central** load, which this is not.

**The Wab/L formula** generalises the familiar central-load case:

| Load position | a, b | M_max |
|---|---|---|
| **Centre** | L/2, L/2 | **WL²/4L = WL/4** ✓ |
| Quarter point | L/4, 3L/4 | 3WL/16 |
| **This case (3/8 span)** | 3, 5 | **15WL/64 = 75 kN·m** |
| Near a support | small a | Small |

> The maximum moment is **greatest when the load is at midspan** and falls as the load moves toward either support — which is why the central position is the critical one for a single moving load.

**The shear and moment diagrams** for this beam:

| Segment | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| Left support to the load | **+25 kN** (constant) | **Linear**, 0 → 75 kN·m |
| At the load | **JUMPS by 40 kN**, 25 → −15 | **Kink** — continuous at 75 |
| Load to right support | **−15 kN** (constant) | **Linear**, 75 → 0 |

**The maximum moment is at the load** because that is where the shear **changes sign** — from +25 to −15. The jump passes through zero, satisfying the condition for a moment extremum.

**Note that the peak moment occurs at a point where V is discontinuous**, not where it is smoothly zero. That is characteristic of point-load problems and is a small extension of the V = 0 rule: the moment peaks wherever the shear **passes through or jumps across zero**.

**MOVING LOADS** are the natural extension, and they matter for bridges and crane girders:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Where is the **absolute maximum moment** for a **single** moving load? | **At midspan**, value **WL/4** |
| Where is the **maximum moment at a GIVEN section**? | When the **load is at that section** |
| Maximum **shear** for a single moving load? | **At a support**, with the load **adjacent** to it, value **W** |

**For a train of loads**, the governing rule is less obvious and worth knowing:

> The **absolute maximum bending moment** occurs under the load nearest the resultant, when the **midspan bisects the distance between that load and the RESULTANT of all the loads on the span**.

**INFLUENCE LINES** are the systematic tool for moving loads:

> An **influence line** plots the value of one **response quantity at one fixed section** as a **unit load moves** across the structure.

| Influence line for | Shape (simply supported span) |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | Linear, 1 at A to 0 at B |
| **Moment at section x** | **Triangular**, peak **ab/L** at x |
| **Shear at section x** | Two parallel lines with a **unit step** at x |

**Do not confuse an influence line with a bending moment diagram:**

| | Bending moment diagram | Influence line |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | **Moment at EVERY section**, for a **FIXED** load | **One quantity at ONE section**, for a **MOVING** unit load |
| Varies with | Position along the beam | Position of the **load** |

They happen to have the same triangular shape for this case, which makes the confusion easy — but they answer entirely different questions.

examTip.trap: 80 kN·m is **WL/4**, the value for a **central** load. This load is not central.
examTip.trick: **M = Wab/L = 40 × 3 × 5/8 = 75 kN·m.** Check via reactions: R_left = Wb/L = 25 kN, and 25 × 3 = 75 ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Wab/L reduces to WL/4 when a = b = L/2** — one formula covers both. The peak sits under the load, because that is where the shear **jumps through** zero.

questions.stem: At an internal hinge in a beam, the condition that makes the structure statically determinate is that the:
questions.solution:
**The bending moment is zero.**

**A hinge transmits shear and axial force but NOT moment**, so it supplies **one additional equation of condition** — and each such equation reduces the degree of static indeterminacy by one.

**Static indeterminacy:**

> **D_s = (number of unknown reactions + internal forces) − (equations of equilibrium + equations of condition)**

For a plane beam: **3 equilibrium equations** (ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, ΣM = 0), plus **one condition equation per internal hinge**.

**Worked examples:**

| Beam | Reactions | Conditions | D_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simply supported | 3 | 0 | **0 — determinate** |
| Cantilever | 3 | 0 | **0 — determinate** |
| **Propped cantilever** | 4 | 0 | **1** |
| **Fixed both ends** | 6 | 0 | **3** |
| Continuous, 3 spans | 5 | 0 | **2** |
| **Fixed both ends with 2 internal hinges** | 6 | **2** | **1** |

**GERBER (hinged) beams** exploit this deliberately:

> Inserting the **right number of hinges in the right places** makes a continuous beam **determinate**, so it can be analysed by statics alone — and, more importantly, so that it is **insensitive to support settlement**.

**That insensitivity is the real engineering motive**, not the ease of analysis:

| Structure | Effect of a support settling |
|---|---|
| **Indeterminate** (continuous) | **Large secondary moments** are induced — potentially exceeding the design moments |
| **DETERMINATE** (Gerber) | **NO stresses induced at all** — the structure simply accommodates the movement |

> A **determinate** structure is **free of self-stress**: settlement, temperature change, shrinkage, creep and lack of fit produce **movement but no force**. An indeterminate one resists the movement and stresses itself doing so.

**Which gives the fundamental trade-off:**

| | **DETERMINATE** | **INDETERMINATE** |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis | **Statics alone** | Needs **compatibility** as well |
| Settlement, temperature, shrinkage | **No stress** | **Induces stress** |
| **Redundancy** | **NONE** — one failure means **collapse** | **Alternative load paths** — failure is contained |
| Material efficiency | Lower | **Higher** — moments are shared and peaks reduced |
| Deflections | Larger | Smaller |

**Redundancy is why most real structures ARE indeterminate**, despite the analytical inconvenience:

> A determinate structure has **exactly enough** members. Lose one and it becomes a **mechanism** — it collapses. An indeterminate structure can **redistribute** load around a failed element, which is the structural basis of **robustness** and the defence against **progressive collapse**.

**Where determinate structures are nevertheless preferred:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Poor or variable founding conditions** | Differential settlement is expected |
| **Long bridges** with large thermal movement | Avoids restraint forces |
| Structures on **mining or subsidence** ground | Movement is certain |
| Where a **simple, checkable analysis** is wanted | — |
| Precast construction with simple connections | Buildability |

**Locating the hinges in a Gerber beam** is not arbitrary: they are placed at the **natural points of contraflexure** of the equivalent continuous beam, so the moment distribution is essentially unchanged while the structure becomes determinate. That gives the efficiency of continuity with the settlement-tolerance of determinacy — an elegant compromise, and the reason the arrangement was used so widely for long bridge girders.

**Kinematic instability** is the trap to avoid: adding **too many** hinges, or placing them badly, turns the structure into a **mechanism**. A beam is unstable if D_s < 0, and it can also be unstable with D_s ≥ 0 if the restraints are badly arranged — for example, three parallel reactions, or three reactions whose lines of action meet at a point. **Counting alone does not prove stability**; the geometry must be checked too.

examTip.trick: A hinge transmits shear and axial force but **not moment**, so it supplies one **equation of condition** and reduces the indeterminacy by one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Determinate structures are FREE OF SELF-STRESS** — settlement, temperature and shrinkage produce movement but no force. That is the real reason for a Gerber beam, not the easier arithmetic. The price is **no redundancy**: one failure is collapse.

questions.stem: An overhanging beam is one which:
options: Has one or both ends projecting beyond the supports
Is supported at the centre only
questions.solution:
**One that has one or both ends projecting beyond its supports.**

**Types of beam by support arrangement:**

| Type | Description | D_s |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | A pin and a roller at the ends | **0** |
| **Cantilever** | **Fixed at one end**, free at the other | **0** |
| **OVERHANGING** | Supports **inboard** of one or both ends | **0** |
| **Propped cantilever** | Fixed one end, simply supported the other | **1** |
| **Fixed (built-in)** | Fixed at both ends | **3** |
| **Continuous** | More than two supports | **(n − 2)** for n supports |

**An overhanging beam is DETERMINATE** — it has only three reaction components, so statics suffices.

**Its characteristic behaviour, and the reason it is used:**

> The overhang produces a **HOGGING (negative) moment** at the support, which **REDUCES the SAGGING moment in the main span**.

**That reduction is a genuine structural benefit:**

| Beam, span L, UDL w | Maximum sagging moment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **wL²/8** |
| With overhangs of **0.207L** each side | **wL²/16** — **halved** |

**The optimum overhang** for a UDL, balancing the hogging and sagging peaks:

> **Overhang ≈ 0.207 L** (that is, L/(2 + 2√2)), giving **equal** hogging and sagging moments of **wL²/16** — **half** the simply supported value.

> Halving the design moment for the same span is a substantial saving, obtained purely by moving the supports inward. It is why cantilevered slab edges, overhanging bridge decks and balanced-cantilever construction are so common.

**Points of contraflexure** are the other characteristic feature: an overhanging beam has the moment **hogging over the support** and **sagging in the span**, so a contraflexure point lies between them — and it locates where the top and bottom reinforcement must each be carried to.

**The practical caution — UPLIFT:**

> If the **overhang is heavily loaded and the main span is not**, the far support can experience **UPLIFT** — a **negative reaction**.

| Consequence | Requirement |
|---|---|
| A **roller or simple bearing cannot resist uplift** | It lifts off |
| The beam may **tip** | Loss of support |
| Design response | **HOLDING-DOWN bolts** or **anchor** at that support, or sufficient dead load |

**Checking for uplift requires the ADVERSE load pattern**, not the full-load case:

> Take **maximum load on the overhang** and **minimum load (dead load only, with the load factor reduced to 0.9) on the main span**. That combination, not the fully loaded one, is what produces uplift.

Analysing only the uniformly loaded case conceals the problem entirely, which is why the pattern-loading check is a code requirement rather than a refinement.

**Where overhanging beams appear:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Balconies and canopies** | The overhang is the useful part |
| **Bridge decks** projecting beyond the outer girders | Reduces the deck's internal moments |
| **Cantilever (balanced) bridge construction** | Built out symmetrically from piers |
| **Crane runway girders** | — |
| Roof purlins over end walls | — |

**Balanced cantilever construction** is the large-scale expression of the principle: segments are built out **symmetrically** from each pier so the hogging moments balance and the pier carries little net moment during construction — then the tips are joined to form a continuous deck. It allows long spans to be built without falsework, which is decisive over deep valleys and rivers.
