questions.stem: The NET IRRIGATION REQUIREMENT of a crop differs from its CONSUMPTIVE USE in that the net irrigation requirement is:
options: The consumptive use LESS the EFFECTIVE RAINFALL and any contribution from the soil moisture store or the groundwater — that is, only the part that irrigation must actually supply
The consumptive use multiplied by the irrigation efficiency
The consumptive use plus the conveyance losses in the canal system
Always equal to the consumptive use
questions.solution:
**The consumptive use LESS the EFFECTIVE RAINFALL and any contribution from the soil moisture store or the groundwater** — that is, only the part that irrigation must actually supply.

**The sequence of quantities, each derived from the one before:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CONSUMPTIVE USE (evapotranspiration, ET)** ← | **The water the crop TRANSPIRES plus what EVAPORATES from the soil surface — the total demand, whatever supplies it** ← |
| **CROP WATER REQUIREMENT** ← | **ET plus any special requirements — puddling and land preparation for paddy, leaching, and losses in the field** ← |
| **NET IRRIGATION REQUIREMENT (NIR)** ← | **Crop water requirement MINUS effective rainfall, minus the contribution from soil moisture and from groundwater** ← |
| **FIELD irrigation requirement** ← | **NIR ÷ the field APPLICATION efficiency** ← |
| **GROSS irrigation requirement (GIR)** ← | **Field requirement ÷ the CONVEYANCE efficiency — the quantity that must be diverted at the head of the system** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM THE FIRST ROW TO THE LAST IS THE WHOLE ARITHMETIC OF IRRIGATION PLANNING AND ITS DIRECTION IS WORTH NOTING: the quantity INCREASES at every step below the third, and DECREASES at the third.**

> **Rainfall reduces what irrigation must supply; inefficiency increases what must be diverted to supply it.**

> **So the gross requirement at the headworks can be two or three times the crop's actual consumptive use, and the difference is entirely rainfall on one side and losses on the other.**

> **Getting the direction of each step right is the commonest arithmetic error in the subject: dividing where one should multiply, or subtracting the rainfall from the gross rather than from the crop requirement, produces an answer wrong by a large factor.**

**THE SOIL MOISTURE AND GROUNDWATER CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE THIRD ROW ARE OFTEN NEGLECTED AND ARE SOMETIMES SUBSTANTIAL:**

| Contribution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Moisture stored in the ROOT ZONE from the previous season** ← | **Particularly at the start of the rabi season, following the monsoon — the soil profile is full, and the first weeks may need no irrigation at all** ← |
| **CAPILLARY RISE from a shallow water table** ← | **Where the water table is within 1 to 2 m of the root zone, it can supply a real fraction of the demand** ← |
| **Neither appears in a simple ET calculation** ← | **So a requirement computed without them OVERSTATES the irrigation needed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS AND IT IS WORTH FOLLOWING: in a waterlogged area the shallow water table supplies much of the crop's need, so the irrigation requirement is genuinely lower.**

> **Continuing to irrigate at the full computed rate then adds water the crop does not need to a profile that is already too wet — which raises the water table further and worsens the waterlogging.**

> **So the failure to account for capillary contribution actively drives the waterlogging problem, and it is one of the mechanisms by which an irrigation scheme damages its own command.**

> **The remedy is to measure the water table and adjust the schedule, which requires observation wells and someone to read them — a modest provision that is regularly omitted.**

**AND THE PADDY EXCEPTION IN THE SECOND ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES A NOTE, SINCE IT DOMINATES NEPALI IRRIGATION:**

> **Paddy is not irrigated to meet an evapotranspiration demand; it is PONDED, and the water requirement is dominated by PERCOLATION through the field's floor and by the puddling water used in land preparation.**

> **So a paddy field's requirement may be 1,000 mm or more against an evapotranspiration of perhaps 500 mm, and the difference is water going into the ground.**

> **That percolation is not entirely lost — it recharges the groundwater and may be pumped again downstream — which is why a basin-scale water accounting gives a very different picture of paddy's water use from a field-scale one.**

> **A field's efficiency of 40 per cent may correspond to a basin efficiency of 80 per cent, because most of the 'loss' returns to the system; and this is why the pursuit of field-level efficiency can be misdirected if the returns are not traced.**

examTip.trick: **ET → crop water requirement → SUBTRACT effective rainfall → NIR → DIVIDE by application efficiency → DIVIDE by conveyance efficiency → GIR.**
examTip.trap: **Rainfall is subtracted at the CROP requirement stage, not from the gross** — and the efficiencies DIVIDE. Getting either direction wrong is wrong by a large factor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capillary rise from a shallow water table supplies real water** — ignoring it over-irrigates land that is already too wet, driving the waterlogging it suffers from.

questions.stem: A crop has a base period of 120 days and the duty of water for it is 1,800 hectares per cumec. The DELTA for the crop is:
questions.solution:
**57.6 cm.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The relation** | **Δ = 8.64 B / D, with Δ in metres, B in days and D in hectares per cumec** ← |
| **Substituting** | **= 8.64 × 120 / 1,800** ← |
| **Numerator** | **= 1,036.8** ← |
| **Δ** | **= 1,036.8 / 1,800 = 0.576 m** ← |
| **In centimetres** | **= 57.6 cm** ← |

> **So the delta is 57.6 cm, that is 576 mm of water depth over the whole base period.**

**THE CONSTANT 8.64 IS A PURE UNIT CONVERSION AND DERIVING IT MAKES THE FORMULA UNFORGETTABLE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **One cumec flowing for one DAY delivers 1 × 86,400 = 86,400 m³** ← | ← |
| **Spread over ONE HECTARE (10,000 m²), that is a depth of 8.64 m** ← | ← |
| **So 1 cumec for B days over D hectares gives a depth of 8.64 B / D metres** ← | **Which is the formula** ← |

> **Anyone who forgets whether the 8.64 goes on top or underneath can rebuild it in fifteen seconds from that observation, which is far more reliable than recalling the arrangement.**

> **And the derivation also settles the UNITS, which is where the other common error lies: the formula gives METRES, so an answer wanted in centimetres must be multiplied by 100, and one wanted in millimetres by 1,000.**

**THE THREE QUANTITIES AND HOW THEY RELATE:**

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DUTY (D)** ← | **The AREA a unit discharge will irrigate — hectares per cumec. A HIGH duty is EFFICIENT: more land from the same water** ← |
| **DELTA (Δ)** ← | **The total DEPTH of water the crop needs over its base period** ← |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** ← | **From the first watering to the last** ← |
| **Their relation** | **Δ = 8.64 B/D, equivalently D = 8.64 B/Δ** ← |

> **THE INVERSE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN DUTY AND DELTA IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE TO HOLD, AND IT FOLLOWS FROM COMMON SENSE: a thirsty crop with a large delta irrigates a small area from a given discharge, so its duty is low.**

> **Paddy has a delta of 1,000 to 1,250 mm and a correspondingly LOW duty; wheat has a delta of about 400 mm and a HIGH duty.**

> **So the two numbers say the same thing from opposite ends, and a candidate confusing them will conclude that paddy is the efficient crop.**

**WHAT MAKES THE DUTY VARY, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL SUBSTANCE:**

| Factor | Effect on duty |
|---|---|
| **The CROP** ← | **The dominant factor — paddy low, wheat and gram high** ← |
| **The CLIMATE** ← | **Hot, dry and windy conditions raise evapotranspiration and LOWER the duty** ← |
| **The SOIL** ← | **A sandy soil percolates heavily, lowering the duty; a clay soil retains water and raises it** ← |
| **The method of APPLICATION** ← | **Wild flooding gives a low duty; furrow, sprinkler and drip progressively higher** ← |
| **The condition of the CANAL** ← | **A lined canal delivers more of what it carries, so the duty AT THE HEAD is higher** ← |
| **Where the duty is MEASURED** ← | **Duty at the FIELD outlet is higher than duty at the canal HEAD, because the losses in between have not yet occurred** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DISTINCTION THAT MUST BE STATED WHENEVER A DUTY IS QUOTED AND IT IS FREQUENTLY OMITTED: a duty figure is meaningless without saying WHERE it applies.**

> **Duty at the field is the crop's own requirement; duty at the outlet includes the distributary losses; duty at the head of the main canal includes everything.**

> **The three differ by a factor approaching two on a leaky system, so comparing a duty from one scheme with a duty from another without establishing the reference point compares nothing at all.**

> **A properly stated figure is therefore 'duty at the head of the distributary' or 'duty at the outlet', and a bare number should be treated with suspicion until its reference is established.**

examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64 B/D = 8.64 × 120/1,800 = 0.576 m = 57.6 cm.** The formula gives METRES.
examTip.trap: **Derive the 8.64: one cumec for one day is 86,400 m³, over one hectare that is 8.64 m depth.** Then the arrangement is obvious rather than remembered.
examTip.mnemonic: **HIGH duty is efficient (more land per cumec), and delta is its inverse** — paddy has a big delta and a low duty. And always state WHERE the duty applies.

questions.stem: EFFECTIVE RAINFALL, in the context of irrigation planning, means:
options: The total rainfall recorded during the crop's growing season
The rainfall that falls only during the daytime

That part of the rainfall which is actually STORED IN THE ROOT ZONE and available to the crop — excluding what runs off, what percolates below the root zone, and what falls when the soil is already at field capacity
The rainfall measured at the nearest meteorological station
questions.solution:
**That part of the rainfall which is actually STORED IN THE ROOT ZONE and available to the crop** — excluding what runs off, what percolates below the root zone, and what falls when the soil is already at field capacity.

**What is lost from the total rainfall before it becomes effective:**

| Loss | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE RUNOFF** ← | **Rain falling faster than the soil can absorb it runs off the field — the more intense the storm, the greater the fraction lost** ← |
| **DEEP PERCOLATION below the root zone** ← | **Water that passes beyond the roots is gone as far as the crop is concerned** ← |
| **Rain falling when the soil is already at FIELD CAPACITY** ← | **The profile cannot hold more, so all of it runs off or percolates** ← |
| **INTERCEPTION by the foliage, evaporating without reaching the soil** ← | **A few millimetres per storm** ← |
| **Rain falling OUTSIDE the growing season** ← | **Except so far as it recharges the profile for the season's start** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE MONSOON'S ENORMOUS RAINFALL IS SO LITTLE USE AGRICULTURALLY: rain is only effective if the soil has ROOM for it.**

> **A soil at field capacity can accept nothing, so a 100 mm storm falling on a saturated profile contributes essentially nothing to the crop.**

> **In Nepal, some 80 per cent of the rain falls in four months and much of it falls on ground already wet — so the effective fraction of the monsoon rainfall is far lower than the totals suggest, and the dry season's small rainfall may be almost entirely effective.**

> **This is why a scheme's water requirement cannot be estimated by subtracting the seasonal rainfall total from the seasonal crop requirement: the effective fraction must be computed month by month, or the requirement will be badly understated.**

**HOW EFFECTIVE RAINFALL IS ESTIMATED:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fixed PERCENTAGE of the total** ← | **Crude — 70 to 80 per cent is sometimes used, and it ignores the intensity and the soil's condition entirely** ← |
| **The USDA Soil Conservation Service method** ← | **A tabulated relationship between monthly rainfall, monthly ET and effective rainfall — the usual practical method** ← |
| **DEPENDABLE rainfall at a stated probability** ← | **Using the 75 or 80 per cent dependable rainfall rather than the average — since a scheme designed on average rainfall FAILS in one year out of two** ← |
| **A daily SOIL WATER BALANCE** ← | **The most accurate — tracking the profile day by day and counting only what it can absorb; laborious by hand and trivial by computer** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS A POINT OF PRINCIPLE THAT APPLIES WELL BEYOND EFFECTIVE RAINFALL AND IT IS WORTH STATING GENERALLY: designing to an AVERAGE means failing half the time.**

> **An irrigation scheme sized on average rainfall will be short of water in every year drier than average, which is half of them.**

> **So the design value is a DEPENDABLE one — typically the rainfall exceeded in 75 or 80 per cent of years — which means the scheme is adequate in four years out of five and short in the fifth.**

> **Choosing that probability is a real decision with a cost: a higher dependability means a larger and dearer scheme, and the appropriate level depends on what the crop is worth and what failure costs the farmer.**

> **For a subsistence crop where failure means hunger, a high dependability is warranted; for a supplementary irrigation improving an already viable rainfed crop, a lower one is rational.**

> **The same reasoning governs the choice of dependable FLOW for the source, and the two must be consistent — a scheme designed on 80 per cent dependable rainfall and 50 per cent dependable river flow has a weakest link that the rainfall assumption conceals.**

examTip.trick: **Only what is stored in the ROOT ZONE and available** — excluding runoff, deep percolation, interception and rain on an already-full profile.
examTip.trap: **Monsoon rain falls largely on wet ground, so its effective fraction is small** — subtracting the seasonal total from the seasonal requirement badly understates the need.
examTip.mnemonic: **Designing to an AVERAGE means failing half the time** — use 75 or 80 % dependable rainfall, and make the dependable FLOW assumption consistent with it.

questions.stem: In an irrigation system the CONVEYANCE efficiency is 70 per cent and the FIELD APPLICATION efficiency is 60 per cent. The OVERALL (project) efficiency is:
questions.solution:
**42 per cent.**

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The efficiencies MULTIPLY, they do not average** ← | **Each acts on what survives the previous one** ← |
| **Overall = 0.70 × 0.60** | **= 0.42** ← |
| **That is** | **42 per cent** ← |

> **So of every 100 units diverted at the headworks, 42 reach the crop's root zone.**

**WHY THEY MULTIPLY IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND OPTION (a) IS THE ERROR IT GUARDS AGAINST:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Divert 100 units at the head** ← | ← |
| **Conveyance at 70 per cent delivers 70 to the field** ← | **30 lost in the canals and watercourses** ← |
| **Application at 60 per cent puts 42 of those 70 into the root zone** ← | **28 lost in the field** ← |
| **So 42 of the original 100 are used** ← | **And the average of 70 and 60 — that is 65 — is meaningless** ← |

> **THE COMPOUNDING IN THE THIRD ROW IS WHY IRRIGATION EFFICIENCY IS SO LOW OVERALL AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: two respectable-sounding efficiencies produce a poor combined result.**

> **And a real system has more than two stages — main canal, branch, distributary, watercourse, field channel, field — each with its own efficiency, all multiplying.**

> **Five stages at 90 per cent each give 0.9⁵ = 59 per cent, so a system in which no single element is bad can still be poor overall.**

> **This is the same multiplicative arithmetic met with fish passes in series, and it has the same implication: improving one stage while the others remain poor achieves proportionately little, and the gains come from raising the WORST stages.**

**THE EFFICIENCIES DEFINED, SINCE THEY ARE EASILY CONFUSED:**

| Efficiency | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **CONVEYANCE, η_c** ← | **Water delivered to the field ÷ water diverted at the head** ← | **60 to 80 per cent unlined; 85 to 95 lined** ← |
| **APPLICATION (farm), η_a** ← | **Water stored in the root zone ÷ water delivered to the field** ← | **40 to 60 per cent surface; 70 to 85 sprinkler; 85 to 95 drip** ← |
| **USE (water use), η_u** ← | **Water USED by the crop ÷ water delivered to the field** ← | ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION, η_d** ← | **A measure of how UNIFORMLY the water is spread over the field — high average depth with poor uniformity still leaves dry patches** ← | ← |
| **OVERALL (project), η_p** ← | **η_c × η_a — this question** ← | **30 to 50 per cent is common** ← |

> **THE DISTRIBUTION EFFICIENCY IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE OF WHAT AVERAGES CONCEAL: a field can receive exactly the right average depth and still have parts under-irrigated.**

> **The farmer, seeing the dry patch, irrigates until THAT patch is wet — which over-irrigates everywhere else.**

> **So poor uniformity forces over-application, and the apparent application efficiency falls for a reason that has nothing to do with the quantity applied and everything to do with how evenly it was spread.**

> **Improving uniformity — by land levelling above all — therefore raises efficiency without any change to the water applied, and LAND LEVELLING is consistently among the most cost-effective irrigation improvements available.**

> **THE COMPARISON IN THE SECOND ROW BETWEEN SURFACE AND DRIP IS WORTH A CLOSING CAUTION, HOWEVER: the field-level gain from drip is real, and the BASIN-level gain may be much smaller.**

> **Water 'lost' to deep percolation from a surface-irrigated field largely recharges the aquifer and is pumped again; water not applied under drip was never diverted.**

> **So converting a scheme to drip saves less water at the basin scale than the field efficiencies suggest, and where the percolation was recharging wells the conversion can reduce the groundwater those wells depend on.**

> **That is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and it is well documented, and it means efficiency improvements should be assessed on a basin water balance rather than on field figures alone.**

examTip.trick: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY: 0.70 × 0.60 = 42 %.** Option (a), 65 %, is their average, which means nothing.
examTip.trap: **Five stages at 90 % each give 59 %** — a system with no single bad element can still be poor. Gains come from raising the WORST stage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Poor UNIFORMITY forces over-application** — the farmer irrigates until the dry patch is wet. Land levelling raises efficiency without changing the water applied.

questions.stem: In irrigation terminology, the CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA) is:
options: The total area lying within the irrigation boundary, including villages, roads and barren land
That part of the GROSS COMMAND AREA which is CULTURABLE — the gross area less the land not fit for cultivation, such as villages, roads, ponds, rock and forest
The area actually irrigated in a particular season
The area that could be irrigated if unlimited water were available
questions.solution:
**That part of the GROSS COMMAND AREA which is CULTURABLE** — the gross area less the land not fit for cultivation, such as villages, roads, ponds, rock and forest.

**The areas, from largest to smallest:**

| Area | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA)** ← | **The TOTAL area that the canal system could command by gravity — everything within its boundary, culturable or not** ← (option a) |
| **CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA)** ← | **GCA MINUS the unculturable land — villages, roads, ponds, rock outcrop, forest, barren ground** ← |
| **Culturable CULTIVATED area** ← | **The part of the CCA actually under cultivation** ← |
| **Culturable UNCULTIVATED area** ← | **Culturable but left fallow** ← |
| **INTENSITY OF IRRIGATION** ← | **The area actually IRRIGATED in a season, as a PERCENTAGE of the CCA** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION MATTERS BECAUSE EVERY IRRIGATION CALCULATION IS BASED ON THE CCA AND NOT THE GCA, AND CONFUSING THEM OVERSTATES THE DEMAND: the roads and villages within the command need no water.**

> **The difference is not trivial — the unculturable fraction may be 15 to 25 per cent of the gross area in a settled plain, and more in broken country.**

> **So a design based on the GCA sizes the canal a fifth too large, and one based on it for a benefit calculation overstates the area that will actually benefit.**

**THE INTENSITY OF IRRIGATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE FIGURE THAT DECIDES THE CANAL'S SIZE AND IT REPAYS UNDERSTANDING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the percentage of the CCA irrigated in a given SEASON** ← | **So there is a kharif intensity and a rabi intensity, and an annual total** ← |
| **It can EXCEED 100 per cent annually** ← | **Because the same land is irrigated in more than one season — 50 per cent in kharif and 50 in rabi gives an annual intensity of 100 per cent** ← |
| **A well-served command may reach 150 or 180 per cent annually** ← | **With two crops on most of the land and three on some** ← |
| **The canal is sized on the SEASONAL peak, not the annual total** ← | **Since the seasons do not overlap** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHERE THE CONFUSION USUALLY ARISES AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: an intensity above 100 per cent does not mean more land than exists.**

> **It means the same land is being cropped more than once a year, which is precisely what irrigation is for — converting a single rainfed monsoon crop into two or three irrigated ones.**

> **So the intensity is a measure of how INTENSIVELY the land is used through the year, and raising it is the scheme's principal benefit.**

> **A scheme that irrigates 100 per cent of its CCA in kharif and nothing in rabi has an annual intensity of 100 per cent and has achieved comparatively little, since kharif is the monsoon season when the crop would largely have grown anyway.**

> **A scheme irrigating 40 per cent in kharif and 60 in rabi has the same annual intensity and has done far more good, because the rabi crop would not have existed without it.**

> **WHICH IS WHY THE SEASONAL BREAKDOWN MATTERS MORE THAN THE ANNUAL TOTAL, AND IT IS THE FIGURE TO ASK FOR: the value of irrigation lies overwhelmingly in the DRY season, when it is the difference between a crop and no crop, rather than in the monsoon, when it is the difference between a crop and a slightly better one.**

> **This has a direct consequence for scheme design in Nepal: a run-of-river irrigation intake with abundant monsoon flow and little dry-season flow delivers water when it is least valuable and fails when it is most — the same seasonal mismatch that afflicts run-of-river hydropower, arising from the same hydrology.**

> **Storage, groundwater conjunctive use, or a source with a dependable dry-season yield are what convert such a scheme from a marginal benefit into a substantial one.**

examTip.trick: **CCA = GCA minus the unculturable land** — villages, roads, ponds, rock, forest. All irrigation calculations use the CCA.
examTip.trap: **Annual intensity can exceed 100 %** — the same land cropped twice. It measures how intensively the land is used through the year, not extra land.
examTip.mnemonic: **The DRY season is where irrigation's value lies** — the difference between a crop and none. A monsoon-only intake delivers when water is least valuable.

questions.stem: The AVAILABLE MOISTURE in a soil, from the point of view of irrigation, is the moisture held between:
options: Saturation and the permanent wilting point

FIELD CAPACITY and the PERMANENT WILTING POINT — the upper limit being what the soil retains against gravity, and the lower the point at which the plant can no longer extract water and does not recover
The hygroscopic coefficient and oven-dry condition
questions.solution:
**FIELD CAPACITY and the PERMANENT WILTING POINT** — the upper limit being what the soil retains against gravity, and the lower the point at which the plant can no longer extract water and does not recover.

**The soil moisture states, from wettest to driest:**

| State | Meaning | Available to the plant? |
|---|---|---|
| **SATURATION** ← | **All the pores full of water; no air** ← | **The excess drains away, and the soil is anaerobic while it lasts** ← |
| **FIELD CAPACITY (FC)** ← | **After free drainage has ceased, typically 1 to 3 days after wetting** ← | **The UPPER limit of useful storage** ← |
| **Between FC and PWP** ← | **Held in the smaller pores and as films** ← | **AVAILABLE — this is the range irrigation manages** ← |
| **PERMANENT WILTING POINT (PWP)** ← | **The plant wilts and does NOT recover even if placed in a humid atmosphere** ← | **The LOWER limit** ← |
| **HYGROSCOPIC water** | **Held so tightly by the soil particles that no plant can extract it** | **NOT available** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE REASON THE UPPER LIMIT IS FIELD CAPACITY AND NOT SATURATION, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: water above field capacity does not stay.**

> **It drains away under gravity within a day or two, and while it is present the soil has no air in it — so the roots cannot respire and the crop is harmed rather than helped.**

> **So irrigating beyond field capacity achieves nothing except deep percolation, a temporary anaerobic condition and a contribution to the water table.**

> **That is the technical statement of why over-irrigation is wasteful AND damaging, and it explains the depth of irrigation calculation: the aim is to refill the profile to field capacity and no further.**

**THE READILY AVAILABLE MOISTURE, WHICH IS WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS SCHEDULING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A plant does NOT extract water equally easily across the whole available range** ← | ← |
| **Near field capacity the water is loosely held and easily taken** ← | ← |
| **Approaching the wilting point it is held ever more tightly, and the plant is under STRESS long before it wilts** ← | ← |
| **So irrigation is scheduled to refill the profile after only a FRACTION of the available moisture has been used** ← | **Commonly 40 to 60 per cent — the READILY available moisture** ← |
| **That fraction is the MANAGEMENT ALLOWED DEPLETION** ← | **And it is chosen by crop sensitivity and by the value of the crop** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL RULE AND IT IS WHY IRRIGATION IS NOT DELAYED UNTIL THE PLANT SHOWS DISTRESS: by the time wilting is visible, yield has already been lost.**

> **A crop under moisture stress closes its stomata, stops photosynthesising and stops growing, and it does so well before any visible symptom appears.**

> **So scheduling by observation of the crop is scheduling too late, and it is why soil moisture measurement — by tensiometer, by gypsum block, by feel and appearance, or by a computed water balance — is worth the trouble.**

> **The choice of depletion fraction also depends on the crop's stage: most crops have CRITICAL PERIODS — flowering and grain filling in particular — during which stress costs disproportionate yield, and a lower depletion is allowed then.**

**THE TYPICAL VALUES, WHICH GIVE THE RANGE ITS PRACTICAL SIZE:**

| Soil | Field capacity | Wilting point | Available moisture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SAND** ← | **About 10 %** | **4 %** | **Only about 6 per cent by weight — a small reservoir, so frequent light irrigation is needed** ← |
| **LOAM** ← | **About 22 %** | **10 %** | **About 12 per cent — the most convenient** ← |
| **CLAY** ← | **About 38 %** | **22 %** | **About 16 per cent — a large reservoir, but the water is held tightly and infiltration is slow** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY THE SOIL DETERMINES THE IRRIGATION SCHEDULE AS MUCH AS THE CROP DOES: a sandy soil holds little, so it must be irrigated often and lightly.**

> **A clay holds much, so it can be irrigated seldom and heavily — but its infiltration rate is low, so applying a heavy depth takes a long time and risks runoff.**

> **So the sandy soil is limited by its STORAGE and the clay by its INFILTRATION, and the irrigation method and interval follow from which limit applies.**

> **That is why a schedule cannot be transferred between fields of different soil, and why a soil survey is part of designing an irrigation scheme rather than an academic preliminary.**

examTip.trick: **Field capacity down to permanent wilting point.** Above field capacity the water drains away within days and the soil is anaerobic meanwhile.
examTip.trap: **Only 40-60 % of that range is READILY available** — the plant is stressed long before it wilts, so irrigation is scheduled on depletion, not on visible symptoms.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sand is limited by STORAGE (irrigate often and lightly); clay by INFILTRATION (seldom and heavily, but slowly).** The schedule follows the soil, not just the crop.

questions.stem: The theoretical POWER available from a hydropower scheme is given by P = ρgQH. For water, using ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s², the power in KILOWATTS for a discharge Q in m³/s and a net head H in metres is:
questions.solution:
**P = 9.81 Q H kilowatts** — and multiplied by the overall efficiency η to give the power actually delivered.

**The derivation, which is worth doing once so the constant is never misremembered:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Mass flow rate** | **= ρQ = 1000 × Q kg/s** ← |
| **Weight flow rate** | **ρgQ = 1000 × 9.81 × Q = 9810 Q newtons per second** ← |
| **Power = weight flow × head** | **P = 9810 Q H watts** ← |
| **In kilowatts** | **P = 9.81 Q H kW** ← |
| **With efficiency** | **P = 9.81 η Q H kW** ← |

> **THE CONSTANT 9.81 IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER AND ITS UNITS ARE THE REASON FOR EVERY MISTAKE MADE WITH THIS FORMULA: it delivers KILOWATTS when Q is in m³/s and H is in metres.**

> **Not watts, not megawatts.**

> **A candidate who writes P = 9.81 × 20 × 100 for a 20 m³/s, 100 m scheme and reports 19,620 watts has made the error; the answer is 19,620 kW, which is 19.6 MW.**

> **Sense-checking against a familiar scheme is the cheapest guard: Kulekhani I is 60 MW, so anything a scheme of similar size produces should land in the tens of megawatts, and an answer in watts or gigawatts is wrong by a factor a thousand either way.**

**A USEFUL APPROXIMATION AND ITS JUSTIFICATION:**

| Approximation | Note |
|---|---|
| **P ≈ 9.81 η Q H, with η typically 0.85 to 0.90 for a good modern plant** ← | ← |
| **9.81 × 0.85 ≈ 8.3, and 9.81 × 0.90 ≈ 8.8** ← | ← |
| **So a rough field figure is P ≈ 8.5 Q H kW** ← | **Which is within a few per cent for most schemes** ← |
| **Or, more roughly still, P ≈ 8 Q H for a first estimate** ← | ← |

> **THE FIGURE 8.5 IS WORTH CARRYING BECAUSE IT LETS A SCHEME BE SIZED MENTALLY, and that is a genuinely useful skill on a site visit: a stream carrying 2 m³/s with 150 m of head available is 8.5 × 2 × 150 ≈ 2,550 kW, which is a 2.5 MW scheme.**

> **That estimate can be made in seconds standing beside the stream, and it decides at once whether the site is worth surveying.**

> **The refinement from 8.5 to the actual efficiency chain — turbine, generator, transformer, penstock losses — changes the answer by perhaps 10 per cent, which does not change the decision.**

> **So the crude estimate does the reconnaissance work and the detailed calculation does the design work, and confusing which is needed at which stage wastes time in both directions.**

**AND THE THREE VARIABLES DESERVE A CLOSING COMMENT ON THEIR RELATIVE STANDING:**

| Variable | Note |
|---|---|
| **H, the HEAD** ← | **Fixed by the topography, and free once found — it costs nothing to have 400 m instead of 40 m** ← |
| **Q, the DISCHARGE** ← | **Fixed by the hydrology, and it varies through the year in a way H does not** ← |
| **η, the EFFICIENCY** ← | **The only one the engineer can influence, and only within a narrow band** ← |

> **The first row is why HIGH HEAD sites are sought above all others, and why Nepal's topography is its hydropower endowment: the head is given by the mountains and costs nothing to obtain beyond the conveyance that reaches it.**

> **A 400 m head site needs a tenth of the discharge of a 40 m site for the same power, which means a tenth of the water, a tenth of the turbine size and a much smaller headworks.**

> **So head is the variable that decides a scheme's economics, and the search for a site is largely a search for head.**

examTip.trick: **P = 9.81 Q H gives KILOWATTS** with Q in m³/s and H in metres — the units of the constant are where every error comes from.
examTip.trap: **Carry 8.5 Q H as the field estimate** — 9.81 times a realistic 0.87 efficiency. It sizes a scheme mentally in seconds beside the stream.
examTip.mnemonic: **Head is free, discharge is given, efficiency is barely adjustable** — which is why high head sites are hunted and why Nepal's mountains are its endowment.

questions.stem: A RUN-OF-RIVER (ROR) hydropower plant is distinguished from a storage plant chiefly in that it:
options: HAS LITTLE OR NO STORAGE, so its output follows the river's natural flow and falls away in the dry season when the flow does
Always generates more energy per unit of installed capacity
Requires no diversion structure at all
Can only be built on rivers with a very small catchment
questions.solution:
**It HAS LITTLE OR NO STORAGE, so its output follows the river's natural flow** — and falls away in the dry season when the flow does.

**The three categories and what separates them:**

| Type | Storage | Output characteristic |
|---|---|---|
| **PURE RUN-OF-RIVER** ← | **None** ← | **Follows the river hour by hour — no control at all** ← |
| **ROR with PONDAGE (peaking ROR)** ← | **A few hours to a day** ← | **Can concentrate the day's flow into the peak hours** ← |
| **STORAGE (reservoir)** ← | **Weeks to a year** ← | **Can shift water from the wet season to the dry, and generate on demand** ← |

> **THE MIDDLE CATEGORY IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD AND IT IS COMMERCIALLY THE MOST IMPORTANT DISTINCTION IN NEPAL: pondage is a small storage — a few hours' worth — that lets the plant hold back the night's flow and release it during the evening peak.**

> **It cannot change the season's total energy at all, because the same water passes through either way.**

> **What it changes is WHEN that energy is delivered, and peak energy is worth considerably more than off-peak energy.**

> **So a peaking ROR plant earns more revenue from the same annual energy than a pure ROR plant, for the cost of a modest pond — which is why almost every new ROR scheme in Nepal is designed with pondage.**

**THE SEASONAL PROBLEM, WHICH IS NEPAL'S CENTRAL HYDROPOWER DIFFICULTY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Nepal's rivers carry perhaps 80 per cent of their annual flow in the four monsoon months** ← | ← |
| **An ROR plant therefore generates at full capacity in the monsoon and at a fraction of it in the dry season** ← | ← |
| **Dry season output can be a fifth or less of the wet season's** ← | ← |
| **But DEMAND does not fall in the dry season — it rises, with lighting load in the long winter evenings** ← | ← |
| **So the country has a surplus when it does not need it and a deficit when it does** ← | ← |
| **Which is exactly the problem STORAGE solves and ROR cannot** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MISMATCH THAT DEFINES NEPAL'S POWER SECTOR AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: building more ROR capacity deepens the mismatch rather than relieving it.**

> **Each new ROR plant adds monsoon energy that must be exported or spilled, and adds only a little dry-season energy.**

> **The dry season deficit is met by imports or by load shedding, and no quantity of ROR capacity changes that.**

> **Only STORAGE — a reservoir that holds monsoon water into the dry season — addresses it, which is why storage projects such as Budhi Gandaki are pursued despite their far greater cost and their far larger displacement and inundation.**

> **So the choice between ROR and storage is not a technical preference but a system-level question, and a country's ROR-to-storage ratio determines whether its generation matches its demand through the year.**

**AND OPTION (a) DESERVES A CORRECTION SINCE IT INVERTS A REAL RELATIONSHIP: an ROR plant typically has a LOWER capacity factor than a storage plant, not a higher one.**

> **Its capacity factor is set by the flow duration curve — it runs at full output only while the river carries the design flow, which may be a few months a year.**

> **A storage plant runs when it is dispatched, so its capacity factor is set by the operator's choice and by the reservoir's yield.**

> **Typical figures are 45 to 60 per cent for an ROR plant in Nepal and rather more for a well-sized storage plant, though a peaking storage plant may deliberately run at a LOW capacity factor while earning a high price — which shows that capacity factor is a description of operation, not a measure of merit.**
tags: monsoon surplus and dry season deficit

examTip.trick: **Little or no storage, so output follows the river** — full in the monsoon, a fifth of that in the dry season.
examTip.trap: **PONDAGE (a few hours) changes WHEN the energy comes, not how much** — the same water passes either way, but peak energy sells for more. Hence almost every new scheme has it.
examTip.mnemonic: **More ROR deepens Nepal's mismatch rather than relieving it** — surplus in the monsoon, deficit in winter when demand peaks. Only storage fixes that.

questions.stem: In hydropower planning, the FIRM POWER (or primary power) of a plant means:
options: The plant's maximum output at full gate opening
The average power delivered over the year
The power the plant can be relied upon to deliver AT ALL TIMES — corresponding to the minimum flow available with the chosen dependability, so that it can be sold under a guaranteed contract
The power delivered during the monsoon months only
questions.solution:
**The power the plant can be relied upon to deliver AT ALL TIMES** — corresponding to the minimum flow available with the chosen dependability, so that it can be sold under a guaranteed contract.

**Firm and secondary power distinguished:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) POWER** ← | **Available at all times, corresponding to the minimum dependable flow — it can be guaranteed** ← |
| **SECONDARY power** ← | **The output above the firm level, available only when the flow exceeds the minimum — it cannot be guaranteed** ← |
| **INSTALLED capacity** ← | **The nameplate rating of the machines, which is reached only at the design flow** ← |
| **AVERAGE power** ← | **The annual energy divided by the hours in the year — a statistic, not a commitment** ← |

> **THE COMMERCIAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS LARGE AND IT IS THE REASON THE DISTINCTION MATTERS: firm power can be sold under a firm contract at a firm price, because the seller can commit to delivering it.**

> **Secondary power can only be sold as and when it happens, at whatever the buyer will pay for unscheduled energy, which is much less.**

> **So two plants with the same annual energy can have very different revenues, depending on how much of that energy is firm.**

> **And a plant's value is therefore raised by anything that raises its firm output — pondage, storage, or a second plant on the same river whose flows are complementary.**

**HOW FIRM POWER IS DETERMINED, WHICH IS WHERE THE FLOW DURATION CURVE ENTERS:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Build the FLOW DURATION CURVE from the long-term daily flow record** ← | **Discharge against the percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded** ← |
| **2. Choose a DEPENDABILITY — commonly Q90, Q95 or the minimum recorded flow** ← | **The flow available 90 or 95 per cent of the time** ← |
| **3. Deduct the RIPARIAN RELEASE required downstream** ← | **In Nepal, 10 per cent of the minimum monthly average flow** ← |
| **4. Compute the power from the remaining flow at the net head** ← | **That is the firm power** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A LEGAL REQUIREMENT THAT IS FREQUENTLY OMITTED FROM A STUDENT'S CALCULATION AND NEVER FROM A REAL ONE: the river must continue to flow below the intake.**

> **Nepal's requirement is the greater of 10 per cent of the minimum monthly average flow or the quantity needed for downstream uses, and it must be released continuously.**

> **In the dry season that release can be a large fraction of the total flow — if the minimum monthly average is 3 m³/s and the current flow is 3.2 m³/s, the plant may take only 2.9 m³/s.**

> **So the riparian release bites hardest exactly when the firm power is being determined, and omitting it overstates the firm power by a proportion that grows as the dry season deepens.**

> **THE SECOND ROW'S CHOICE OF DEPENDABILITY IS A COMMERCIAL DECISION DRESSED AS A TECHNICAL ONE AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING AS SUCH: a higher dependability means a lower firm power but a firmer commitment.**

> **Q95 gives less firm power than Q90 but fails only 5 per cent of the time rather than 10.**

> **Which is chosen depends on the penalty for failing to deliver, and that is written into the power purchase agreement rather than into any engineering standard.**

> **So the engineer supplies the flow duration curve and the consequences of each choice, and the choice itself belongs to whoever bears the contractual risk.**

examTip.trick: **Available at all times — the minimum dependable flow** — so it can be sold under a guaranteed contract. Everything above it is secondary power.
examTip.trap: **Deduct the RIPARIAN RELEASE before computing firm power** — Nepal requires 10% of the minimum monthly average flow, and it bites hardest in the dry season.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two plants, same annual energy, very different revenue** — the split between firm and secondary decides it. Pondage and storage buy firmness.

questions.stem: The FLOW DURATION CURVE used in hydropower planning plots:
options: Discharge against time in chronological order through the year
Discharge against the corresponding water level
DISCHARGE against the PERCENTAGE OF TIME that discharge is equalled or exceeded — which discards the chronological order and answers instead how often each flow is available
questions.solution:
**DISCHARGE against the PERCENTAGE OF TIME that discharge is equalled or exceeded** — which discards the chronological order and answers instead how often each flow is available.

**How it is constructed and what it shows:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Take the daily (or ten-daily) flow record over as many years as exist** ← | **Twenty years or more is desirable** ← |
| **2. RANK every value from largest to smallest, ignoring when it occurred** ← | ← |
| **3. Assign each an exceedance percentage: P = m/(N+1) × 100, m being the rank** ← | ← |
| **4. Plot discharge against P** ← | **Conventionally with discharge on the vertical axis** ← |
| **The result descends from left to right** ← | **High flows rare on the left, low flows common on the right** ← |

> **THE SECOND STEP IS THE CURVE'S ESSENTIAL PROPERTY AND ITS ESSENTIAL LIMITATION AT THE SAME TIME: the chronological order is thrown away.**

> **The curve tells you that a flow of 5 m³/s is exceeded 60 per cent of the time; it does not tell you whether those 60 per cent are a continuous six-month wet season or are scattered through the year.**

> **For an ROR plant with no storage that does not matter, because the plant simply takes what arrives each day and the curve captures exactly that.**

> **For a plant with STORAGE it matters entirely, because storage works by moving water from one time to another, and a curve with no time axis cannot represent that.**

> **So the flow duration curve is the correct tool for ROR planning and the WRONG tool for reservoir sizing — which requires the chronological hydrograph, or a mass curve derived from it.**

**WHAT THE CURVE'S SHAPE REVEALS:**

| Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **STEEP curve** ← | **Highly variable flow — flashy catchment, little groundwater or snow contribution** ← |
| **FLAT curve** ← | **Well-regulated flow — large groundwater storage, snowmelt, or an upstream lake** ← |
| **A flat TAIL on the right** ← | **A good sustained dry-season flow, which is what firm power depends on** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHAT A HYDROPOWER PLANNER LOOKS AT FIRST AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY: the right-hand end of the curve determines the firm power, and the firm power determines much of the revenue.**

> **Two catchments with the same mean annual flow can have very different tails — one draining a snowfed high catchment with a sustained spring melt, the other a rain-fed hill catchment that nearly dries.**

> **The snowfed one is much the better hydropower site, though the two look identical on an annual water balance.**

> **So the mean annual flow is almost useless for site selection and the flow duration curve is almost sufficient, which is why the curve is drawn before anything else is decided.**

**AND THE DESIGN DISCHARGE IS CHOSEN ON THIS CURVE, WHICH IS ITS OTHER MAIN USE:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A design flow at Q40 gives a large plant that runs at full output only 40 per cent of the time** ← | **High capacity, low capacity factor, high capital cost** ← |
| **A design flow at Q80 gives a small plant that runs at full output most of the year** ← | **Low capacity, high capacity factor, low capital cost** ← |
| **The optimum is where the marginal energy gained stops paying for the marginal capacity added** ← | ← |
| **In Nepal, Q40 to Q50 is a common choice for an ROR scheme** ← | **Though it depends on the tariff structure and the curve's own shape** ← |

> **The third row is the optimisation and it is genuinely an economic calculation rather than a rule: each increment of installed capacity costs a known amount and earns the energy lying under that slice of the curve.**

> **Where the slice is thin — far to the left, where the high flows are rare — the energy earned is small and the capacity still costs full price.**

> **So the curve is worked leftward until the increments stop paying, and where that point falls depends on the curve's steepness and on what the energy is worth.**

examTip.trick: **Discharge against the per cent of time it is equalled or exceeded** — ranked, with the chronology thrown away.
examTip.trap: **Right for ROR, WRONG for reservoir sizing** — storage moves water through time, and a curve with no time axis cannot represent that. Use the mass curve instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **The right-hand TAIL sets the firm power** — two catchments with equal mean flow can have utterly different tails, and the snowfed one is the better site.

questions.stem: The CAPACITY FACTOR (plant factor) of a hydropower plant is defined as:
options: The ratio of the ACTUAL ENERGY generated in a period to the energy that would have been generated had the plant run at its INSTALLED CAPACITY throughout that period
Peak output divided by firm output
Installed capacity divided by the maximum demand on the system
The ratio of firm power to installed capacity
questions.solution:
**The ratio of the ACTUAL ENERGY generated in a period to the energy that would have been generated had the plant run at its INSTALLED CAPACITY throughout that period.**

**Stated as a formula and worked through:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Capacity factor** | **CF = actual energy in the period ÷ (installed capacity × hours in the period)** ← |
| **For a year** | **CF = annual energy (kWh) ÷ (installed capacity in kW × 8760)** ← |
| **Example** | **A 10 MW plant generating 48 GWh in a year** ← |
| **Denominator** | **10,000 kW × 8760 h = 87.6 GWh** ← |
| **So** | **CF = 48 ÷ 87.6 = 0.548, or about 55 per cent** ← |

> **THE 8760 IS THE NUMBER TO HAVE READY AND IT IS SIMPLY 365 × 24, and having it available turns this calculation into a few seconds of arithmetic.**

> **A related figure worth carrying is that 1 MW running continuously for a year produces 8.76 GWh, so a plant's annual energy in GWh divided by 8.76 gives the megawatts it would need to run flat out.**

> **Divide that by the installed capacity and the capacity factor falls out.**

> **For the example: 48 ÷ 8.76 = 5.48 MW equivalent continuous, against 10 MW installed, giving 0.548 — the same answer by a shorter route.**

**WHY A HYDROPOWER PLANT'S CAPACITY FACTOR IS WHAT IT IS:**

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The river's flow falls below the design flow for much of the year** ← | **The dominant cause for an ROR plant** ← |
| **Outages for maintenance and repair** ← | **A few per cent** ← |
| **Transmission constraints or a system unable to absorb the output** ← | **Can be substantial where the grid is weak** ← |
| **Deliberate PEAKING operation** ← | **A storage plant may run only at peak hours by design** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CAUTION THAT MAKES CAPACITY FACTOR A POOR MEASURE OF MERIT AND IT IS OFTEN MISUSED IN EXACTLY THIS WAY: a low capacity factor may indicate a badly conceived plant or a deliberately valuable one.**

> **A peaking plant that runs four hours a day at a high tariff has a capacity factor near 0.17 and may be the most profitable plant on the system.**

> **An ROR plant with a capacity factor of 0.60 selling at a flat tariff may earn less per rupee invested.**

> **So capacity factor describes how a plant is operated and reveals nothing by itself about whether it is a good plant, and comparing two plants by capacity factor alone is a mistake that is made frequently in policy discussion.**

**AND TWO NEIGHBOURING TERMS ARE WORTH DISTINGUISHING SINCE THEY ARE ROUTINELY CONFUSED:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CAPACITY (plant) FACTOR** ← | **Actual energy ÷ (installed capacity × period) — as above** ← |
| **LOAD FACTOR** ← | **Average load ÷ PEAK load, over a period — a property of the DEMAND, not the plant** ← |
| **UTILISATION FACTOR** ← | **Maximum load actually served ÷ installed capacity — how fully the plant's capacity is ever used** ← |
| **AVAILABILITY FACTOR** ← | **Time the plant was AVAILABLE to run ÷ total time — excludes outages but not idle capacity** ← |

> **The second row is the one most confused with the first, and the distinction is which side of the meter the quantity describes: load factor describes the DEMAND's shape and capacity factor describes the PLANT's output.**

> **A system with a poor load factor — a sharp evening peak and a low night load — needs peaking plant, which will itself run at a low capacity factor.**

> **So the two are related through the system's design, and a country whose load factor is poor should expect some of its plant to have low capacity factors, by design rather than by failure.**

examTip.trick: **Actual energy ÷ (installed capacity × 8760)** for a year. And 1 MW flat out for a year = 8.76 GWh, which shortens every such sum.
examTip.trap: **A low capacity factor is not a fault** — a peaking plant running four hours a day at 0.17 may be the most profitable on the system.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capacity factor describes the PLANT; load factor describes the DEMAND** — average load over peak load, on the other side of the meter.

questions.stem: In the sequence of studies for a hydropower project, a PRE-FEASIBILITY STUDY differs from a FEASIBILITY STUDY principally in that the pre-feasibility study:
options: Includes the detailed design drawings and the tender documents

Uses EXISTING and rapidly-collected data to compare ALTERNATIVES and establish whether the project merits further study — while the feasibility study investigates the SELECTED alternative in depth and to a cost accuracy sufficient for an investment decision
Is carried out after construction has begun
Is required only for projects above 100 MW
questions.solution:
**It uses EXISTING and rapidly-collected data to compare ALTERNATIVES and establish whether the project merits further study** — while the feasibility study investigates the SELECTED alternative in depth and to a cost accuracy sufficient for an investment decision.

**The study sequence in full:**

| Stage | Purpose and depth |
|---|---|
| **RECONNAISSANCE / desk study** ← | **Maps, existing records, a site visit. Identifies candidate sites. Cost accuracy ±40% or worse** ← |
| **PRE-FEASIBILITY** ← | **Compares ALTERNATIVES — layouts, headworks sites, capacities. Selects one. Cost accuracy ±25 to 30%** ← |
| **FEASIBILITY** ← | **Investigates the SELECTED scheme in depth — drilling, gauging, seismic, EIA, financial model. Cost accuracy ±10 to 15%** ← |
| **DETAILED DESIGN / tender design** ← | **Drawings, specifications, bills of quantities. Cost accuracy ±5 to 10%** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION drawings** ← | **Issued as the work proceeds, incorporating what the excavation reveals** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW'S PURPOSE — COMPARING ALTERNATIVES — IS WHAT MOST DISTINGUISHES IT AND IT IS THE STAGE MOST OFTEN SKIPPED: a pre-feasibility study should examine several layouts and select among them.**

> **Where the intake goes, whether the conveyance is a canal or a tunnel, which bank it runs on, how high the dam is, what capacity is installed.**

> **Each combination is costed roughly and the best is carried forward.**

> **Skipping this stage — going from reconnaissance straight to a feasibility study of one layout — means the layout studied was chosen by someone's judgement rather than by comparison, and it may well not be the best.**

> **A layout error discovered at feasibility stage is expensive to correct and one discovered during construction is usually not corrected at all, so the cheap comparative work at pre-feasibility stage is where the largest savings are available.**

**THE COST ACCURACY COLUMN DESERVES ATTENTION BECAUSE IT IS ROUTINELY IGNORED WHEN THE FIGURES ARE QUOTED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A pre-feasibility cost of 'Rs 4 billion' means Rs 3 to 5 billion** ← | ← |
| **Quoting it as Rs 4 billion, without the range, creates a false expectation** ← | ← |
| **Which the feasibility study's more accurate Rs 4.6 billion then appears to violate** ← | ← |
| **And the project acquires a reputation for cost overrun before any work has begun** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES A GENUINE AND COMMON INJUSTICE TO PROJECTS AND IT IS AVOIDABLE BY DISCIPLINE IN REPORTING: every cost estimate should be quoted with its accuracy and its base date.**

> **'Rs 4.0 billion ± 30 per cent, at 2026 prices' is an honest statement and 'Rs 4 billion' is not, though they rest on identical work.**

> **The discipline costs nothing and it protects both the estimator and the project, because a later estimate within the stated range is then a confirmation rather than an overrun.**

> **And where a project genuinely does overrun, the discipline makes that visible too, which is the point of it.**

**A CLOSING NOTE ON THE RELATIVE COSTS OF THE STAGES, WHICH IS ENCOURAGING:**

> **The whole investigation sequence — reconnaissance through detailed design — typically costs 3 to 8 per cent of the project's construction cost.**

> **The decisions it informs determine essentially all of that cost.**

> **So investigation is the highest-leverage expenditure on a project, and economising on it in order to start construction sooner is the least defensible economy available — it saves a small certain amount and risks a large uncertain one.**

> **The counter-pressure is real, though: investigation produces no visible progress, and a sponsor under pressure to show activity finds it the easiest budget to cut.**

examTip.trick: **Pre-feasibility COMPARES alternatives and selects one; feasibility investigates that one in depth** — ±25-30% against ±10-15% cost accuracy.
examTip.trap: **Skipping pre-feasibility means the layout was chosen by judgement, not comparison** — and a layout error found later is rarely corrected at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quote every estimate with its range and base date** — 'Rs 4.0 bn ± 30%, 2026 prices'. Without it, a more accurate later figure looks like an overrun.

questions.stem: For a hydropower project in Nepal, the environmental study required — IEE or EIA — is determined principally by:
options: The developer's own assessment of the likely impacts
Whether the project is publicly or privately financed
The length of the transmission line only
The project's INSTALLED CAPACITY, together with whether it lies in a protected area — with an IEE for smaller projects and a full EIA for larger ones or for any project in a sensitive area
questions.solution:
**The project's INSTALLED CAPACITY, together with whether it lies in a protected area** — with an IEE for smaller projects and a full EIA for larger ones or for any project in a sensitive area.

**How the threshold system works:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The Environment Protection Act and its Rules SCHEDULE the projects requiring each level** ← | ← |
| **Schedule 1 lists projects requiring a BRIEF ENVIRONMENTAL STUDY or an IEE** ← | **Initial Environmental Examination** ← |
| **Schedule 2 lists those requiring a full EIA** ← | ← |
| **For hydropower the criterion is INSTALLED CAPACITY in MW** ← | **With the thresholds set in the Rules and revised from time to time** ← |
| **And ANY project within a national park, reserve or conservation area requires an EIA** ← | **Regardless of its size** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN OVERRIDE THAT CATCHES DEVELOPERS OUT AND IT IS WORTH CHECKING EARLY: a 2 MW scheme that would otherwise need only an IEE requires a full EIA if it falls inside a protected area.**

> **Nepal's protected areas cover a substantial part of the country and much of it is precisely the steep high-head terrain that suits hydropower.**

> **So the boundary check is a first-day task on any site, and it changes the study's cost and duration by a large factor — an EIA takes a year or more where an IEE may take a few months.**

> **Discovering the requirement late, after an IEE has been prepared, wastes that work entirely and delays the project by the EIA's full duration.**

**THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO STUDIES IN PRACTICE:**

| Aspect | IEE | EIA |
|---|---|---|
| **Scoping** | **Not required separately** ← | **A scoping document and Terms of Reference must be APPROVED first** ← |
| **Public participation** | **A public notice and local consultation** ← | **Public notice, public hearing, and wider consultation** ← |
| **Baseline data** | **Largely existing data with limited field survey** ← | **A full seasonal baseline — often a year's data** ← |
| **Approving authority** | **The concerned ministry** ← | **The Ministry of Forests and Environment** ← |
| **Typical duration** | **A few months** ← | **A year or more** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE LARGEST DRIVER OF AN EIA'S DURATION AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED IN A PROJECT PROGRAMME: a seasonal biological baseline cannot be compressed.**

> **Aquatic life, migratory fish, breeding birds and the seasonal use of the river by people all require observation across the year, and no amount of resource shortens it.**

> **A programme that allows three months for an EIA has not understood this, and the project will wait.**

> **The way to protect the programme is to start the baseline collection EARLY — during pre-feasibility, before the EIA is formally commissioned — so that when the study begins the data already exists.**

> **That is a small expenditure made a year before it is needed, and it is one of the few ways to genuinely shorten a project's development period rather than merely compressing its later stages.**

**AND THE ENVIRONMENTAL STUDY'S OUTPUT DESERVES A NOTE, SINCE ITS PURPOSE IS OFTEN MISCONCEIVED AS A PERMIT:**

> **An approved EIA is not merely a clearance; it contains an ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN with commitments that become binding obligations.**

> **Riparian releases, fish passage, spoil disposal locations, dust and noise limits, restoration of borrow areas, and a monitoring and reporting regime.**

> **Those commitments cost money to honour and they must be in the project's budget and its contracts, not merely in its EIA report.**

> **A common and serious failure is an EIA whose commitments were never transmitted to the construction contract — so the contractor is not required to do what the project promised, and the project is in breach through nobody's deliberate decision.**
tags: EMP commitments must reach the contract

examTip.trick: **Installed capacity sets the level — IEE for small, EIA for large** — with the thresholds in the Environment Protection Rules.
examTip.trap: **Any project inside a protected area needs a full EIA regardless of size** — and Nepal's protected areas cover much of the best high-head terrain. Check the boundary on day one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Start the seasonal baseline EARLY, during pre-feasibility** — a year of biological data cannot be compressed by any amount of resource.

questions.stem: A PUMPED STORAGE plant is best described as a scheme that:
options: PUMPS water from a lower to an upper reservoir using cheap off-peak energy and generates from it at peak — consuming more energy than it returns, and existing to shift energy in TIME rather than to produce it
Pumps groundwater to supplement a river's dry-season flow
Uses a pump instead of a turbine to generate power
Pumps water over a ridge into an adjacent, steeper catchment
questions.solution:
**It PUMPS water from a lower to an upper reservoir using cheap off-peak energy and generates from it at peak** — consuming more energy than it returns, and existing to shift energy in TIME rather than to produce it.

**How the economics work despite the net loss:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Round-trip efficiency is typically 70 to 80 per cent** ← | **So 100 units pumped return 75 units** ← |
| **The plant is therefore a NET CONSUMER of energy** ← | ← |
| **But it buys at the OFF-PEAK price and sells at the PEAK price** ← | ← |
| **If the peak price is more than about 1.35 times the off-peak price, it profits** ← | **1 ÷ 0.75 = 1.33, plus a margin** ← |
| **So its viability depends entirely on the PRICE SPREAD, not on any energy gain** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE WHOLE COMMERCIAL CASE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING CLEARLY BECAUSE IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: a device that destroys a quarter of the energy passing through it is profitable because the energy it destroys was cheap and the energy it delivers is dear.**

> **This is arbitrage, and it is no different in principle from buying grain at harvest and selling it in the lean season, allowing for the losses in the store.**

> **The store loses grain and still pays, because the price difference exceeds the loss.**

> **So a pumped storage plant should be understood as a STORE rather than as a generator, and judging it by its efficiency is as beside the point as judging a warehouse by its shrinkage.**

**WHY PUMPED STORAGE MATTERS INCREASINGLY, AND PARTICULARLY FOR NEPAL:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the only mature LARGE-SCALE electricity storage technology** ← | **Batteries are growing but remain smaller and shorter-duration** ← |
| **It provides fast response for frequency regulation and reserve** ← | **A pumped storage unit can go from standstill to full output in minutes** ← |
| **It absorbs surplus generation that would otherwise be spilled** ← | ← |
| **Which is exactly Nepal's monsoon situation** ← | **Surplus ROR generation with nowhere to go** ← |
| **And it can turn that surplus into dry-season peak energy** ← | **If the upper reservoir is large enough to store seasonally** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CARRIES A LARGE CONDITION AND IT IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES WHETHER PUMPED STORAGE ADDRESSES NEPAL'S PROBLEM OR MERELY ITS DAILY ONE: most pumped storage plants cycle DAILY, with a reservoir holding six to twelve hours of generation.**

> **That shifts energy from night to evening, which is useful and is what the technology is normally built for.**

> **Shifting energy from the monsoon to the dry season needs a reservoir holding MONTHS of generation, which is a vastly larger structure and is really a conventional storage reservoir that happens to be filled by pumping.**

> **So pumped storage as normally conceived helps Nepal's daily peak problem and does very little for its seasonal one, and conflating the two overstates what the technology offers.**

> **The honest statement is that pumped storage is a strong answer to the daily peak and to grid stability as variable renewables grow, and that the seasonal deficit still requires conventional storage or imports.**

**A NOTE ON THE PHYSICAL ARRANGEMENT, WHICH IS SIMPLER THAN IT SOUNDS:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **An UPPER and a LOWER reservoir, with as much head between them as the site allows** ← | ← |
| **A waterway connecting them** ← | ← |
| **REVERSIBLE PUMP-TURBINES, which run one way to generate and the other to pump** ← | **A single machine doing both, which halves the plant cost** ← |
| **A motor-generator, likewise reversible** ← | ← |

> **The third row is the technology that made pumped storage economic: a Francis runner run in reverse works acceptably as a pump, so one machine serves both duties.**

> **Separate pumps and turbines were used in early schemes and doubled the machine hall.**

> **The reversible machine is a compromise — it is not quite the optimum shape for either duty — and the small efficiency penalty is repaid many times over in capital cost, which is a trade worth recognising as a general one.**

examTip.trick: **Pump off-peak, generate at peak** — a net CONSUMER of energy at 70-80% round trip, profitable purely on the price spread.
examTip.trap: **Judge it as a STORE, not a generator** — like a grain warehouse, it loses stock and still pays because the price difference exceeds the loss.
examTip.mnemonic: **Most schemes cycle DAILY, not seasonally** — so pumped storage answers Nepal's evening peak, not its dry-season deficit. Don't conflate the two.

questions.stem: In Nepal's hydropower licensing regime administered by the Department of Electricity Development, a SURVEY LICENSE:
options: Permits construction to begin while the studies are completed in parallel

Grants the exclusive right to INVESTIGATE a specified river reach for a limited period — during which the holder prepares the studies, and after which a separate GENERATION LICENSE must be obtained before construction
Is issued only after the environmental study has been approved
Grants the holder permanent water rights over the river reach
questions.solution:
**It grants the exclusive right to INVESTIGATE a specified river reach for a limited period** — during which the holder prepares the studies, and after which a separate GENERATION LICENSE must be obtained before construction.

**The two licenses and what each permits:**

| License | Grants | Typical term |
|---|---|---|
| **SURVEY license** ← | **The exclusive right to study a defined reach — access, gauging, drilling, topographic survey** ← | **A few years, extendable** ← |
| **GENERATION license** ← | **The right to build and operate, and to use the water** ← | **Decades, after which the plant transfers to the state** ← |

> **THE WORD 'EXCLUSIVE' IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE LICENSE'S WHOLE COMMERCIAL VALUE AND IT IS WHY THE SYSTEM EXISTS: studying a site costs a great deal and produces information that anyone could then use.**

> **Without exclusivity nobody would invest in the studies, because a competitor could wait for the results and then bid for the site with no investigation cost of their own.**

> **The survey license solves that by reserving the site to whoever is doing the work, for long enough to complete it and to apply for generation.**

> **It is a straightforward answer to a free-rider problem, and it is the same device used in mineral exploration for exactly the same reason.**

**THE SYSTEM'S CHARACTERISTIC ABUSE, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A survey license is cheap to obtain relative to the site's value** ← | ← |
| **So licenses have been taken out with no intention of developing** ← | ← |
| **Held, and then sold on to a genuine developer at a large mark-up** ← | **The practice known as license trading or site squatting** ← |
| **Which delays development and adds a cost that produces nothing** ← | ← |
| **The regulatory answers are performance BONDS, strict MILESTONES and non-transferability** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW LISTS THE STANDARD REMEDIES AND THE MILESTONE CONDITION IS THE MOST EFFECTIVE OF THEM: the license requires specified progress by specified dates, and lapses if the progress is not made.**

> **A holder with no intention of developing cannot meet the milestones and loses the license, while a genuine developer meets them in the ordinary course of the work.**

> **The condition therefore discriminates between the two at no cost to the honest party, which is what a good regulatory test does.**

> **The difficulty is enforcement — declaring a license lapsed invites litigation, and an agency that hesitates to do so leaves the milestones unenforced and the abuse unaddressed.**

**AND THE GENERATION LICENSE'S TERM DESERVES A CLOSING WORD BECAUSE IT SHAPES THE WHOLE FINANCIAL MODEL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The license runs for a defined period, after which the plant transfers to the Government** ← | **A build-own-operate-transfer arrangement** ← |
| **So the developer must recover the entire investment WITHIN that period** ← | ← |
| **Which sets the tariff, the debt tenor and the required return** ← | ← |
| **And makes any DELAY costly twice over — interest during construction, and a shortened earning period** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row is why delay is so damaging to a hydropower project's economics and it is worth stating precisely: the license term generally runs from its issue, not from commissioning.**

> **So a project delayed three years has three fewer years of revenue at the end, in addition to having paid three years of interest on undeployed capital.**

> **The two effects compound, and a delay that appears to cost only its financing charge in fact costs that plus the most valuable years of the concession — the late ones, when the debt is repaid and the revenue is nearly all margin.**

> **That is why developers press so hard on approvals and why the licensing timetable, which looks like an administrative matter, is in fact a first-order determinant of whether projects get built.**

examTip.trick: **Survey license = exclusive right to STUDY a reach; generation license = right to BUILD and operate** — two separate instruments, in that order.
examTip.trap: **Exclusivity exists to defeat free riding** — without it nobody funds studies a competitor could use for free. Same device as mineral exploration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Delay costs twice** — interest during construction, plus the loss of the concession's last and most profitable years, since the term runs from issue not commissioning.

questions.stem: The GROSS HEAD of a hydropower plant is the difference in level between the headwater and tailwater surfaces. The NET HEAD used in the power calculation is the gross head less:
options: ALL HYDRAULIC LOSSES in the water conveyance system — the intake, the headrace, the settling basin, the forebay, the penstock and its bends and valves — since only the head remaining at the turbine can do work
questions.solution:
**ALL HYDRAULIC LOSSES in the water conveyance system** — the intake, the headrace, the settling basin, the forebay, the penstock and its bends and valves — since only the head remaining at the turbine can do work.

**The head accounting, from the reservoir down:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **GROSS head — headwater level minus tailwater level** ← | **The total available drop** ← |
| **Less: intake and trashrack losses** ← | **Small, but rising as the rack fouls** ← |
| **Less: headrace (canal or tunnel) friction** ← | **Often the largest single loss on a long conveyance** ← |
| **Less: settling basin and forebay losses** ← | ← |
| **Less: penstock friction, bends, valves, contractions** ← | ← |
| **= NET head, which is what P = 9.81 η Q H uses** ← | ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN HYDRAULIC LOSSES AND MACHINE LOSSES IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND KEEPING THEM SEPARATE PREVENTS DOUBLE-COUNTING: hydraulic losses reduce the HEAD, and machine losses reduce the EFFICIENCY.**

> **They enter the power equation at different places — the head losses inside H and the machine losses inside η.**

> **Deducting turbine losses from the head as well as applying the turbine efficiency counts them twice, which is a common slip.**

> **The clean rule is: everything the WATER loses on its way to the runner comes off the head, and everything the MACHINERY loses after that comes off the efficiency.**

**HOW LARGE THE LOSSES SHOULD BE ALLOWED TO GET, WHICH IS A DESIGN DECISION RATHER THAN A GIVEN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Total conveyance losses are commonly designed to 3 to 8 per cent of gross head** ← | ← |
| **A larger conveyance costs more and loses less** ← | ← |
| **So the optimum diameter is where the marginal cost of enlarging equals the marginal value of the head saved** ← | ← |
| **Which is the classic penstock diameter optimisation** ← | ← |
| **And it depends on the tariff — dearer energy justifies a larger pipe** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A RELATIONSHIP WORTH CARRYING BECAUSE IT SURPRISES PEOPLE: the correct penstock diameter is not a property of the hydraulics alone.**

> **The same flow, head and length in a country with a high energy price justifies a larger, more expensive pipe than in a country with a low one, because the head saved is worth more.**

> **So a penstock designed to a foreign standard's loss allowance may be the wrong size for the local tariff, in either direction.**

> **The calculation is not difficult and it should be done for each project rather than taken from a rule, because the answer moves with the energy price and the steel price, both of which change.**

**AND A PRACTICAL WARNING ABOUT THE TAILWATER LEVEL, WHICH IS THE GROSS HEAD'S NEGLECTED HALF:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tailwater level RISES when the river is in flood** ← | ← |
| **Which reduces the gross head exactly when the flow is greatest** ← | ← |
| **So a plant may lose head at the moment it has most water** ← | ← |
| **And for a low-head plant this effect can be severe — a 5 m rise on a 12 m head is crippling** ← | ← |
| **For a high-head plant it is negligible — 5 m on 400 m is nothing** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS SET OUT WHY TAILWATER MATTERS AT LOW HEAD AND NOT AT HIGH HEAD, and it is a proportional argument rather than an absolute one.**

> **So the tailwater rating curve is an essential input for a low-head plant's energy calculation and a footnote for a high-head one.**

> **Neglecting it on a low-head scheme overstates the monsoon energy substantially, because it applies the dry-season head to the monsoon flows — which is precisely the combination that never occurs.**

examTip.trick: **Gross head less ALL hydraulic losses in the conveyance** — intake, headrace, basin, forebay, penstock.
examTip.trap: **Water losses come off the HEAD; machine losses come off the EFFICIENCY** — deducting turbine losses from head as well as applying η counts them twice.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tailwater rises in flood, cutting the head when the flow is greatest** — crippling on a 12 m head, nothing on 400 m.
